A fault at that boundary could be relevant to either question, so neither check substitutes for the other.
Should I describe the injection as testing linearizability in its entirety?

It is more precise to name the stated checks: stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival across fencing, reconciliation, and promotion. Those are important to linearizable, crash-safe ownership transfer, but this activity does not say that every aspect of linearizability or every client operation history is being checked.
And does it test retry deduplication explicitly?

The activity does not say so. Retries could matter to an ownership transfer, but the named checks here are stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival under partition and crash injection. We should not describe this run as an explicit retry-deduplication test without more information.
Does running the injections establish that the old-quorum fence works under partitions?

Running them creates an opportunity to observe that behavior in the tested 3+3-replica setup. The activity does not report the observations, so it does not establish a passing result. In interpreting any result, the relevant question is whether the old side can successfully acknowledge under stale authority, including when a partition prevents prompt communication.
Can this activity tell me whether the migration meets the 80% throughput target under continuous writes?

No throughput result is stated. This activity injects partitions and crashes around fencing, reconciliation, and promotion and checks two safety properties. The separate target concerns sustaining at least 80% of migration-free throughput without failures while migrating a shard under continuous writes; no measurement against that target appears here.
What can I responsibly say about the fault-injection effort right now?

You can say that 3+3-replica partition and crash fault injection is being run across fencing, reconciliation, and promotion, with checks for stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival. That preserves both the test scope and its purpose without claiming a pass, a failure, or coverage beyond the stated activity.

The fault injection found a problematic schedule: in 1/10,000 injected schedules, delayed pre-fence replication replies let the old leader acknowledge a write after promotion, and the destination missed that write.

That is a concrete safety failure in the observed schedule. The acknowledgment happened after promotion even though the replies it relied on were associated with pre-fence replication, and the destination did not have the acknowledged write. The reported frequency is one occurrence among 10,000 injected schedules; it is not, by itself, an estimate of how often this would happen in production.
Why does the timing of the replication replies matter so much?

Because a reply associated with work before the fence can be delivered later. In this schedule, the old leader was able to use delayed pre-fence replies to acknowledge after promotion. The distinction between when replication work occurred and when the leader issued an acknowledgment matters at the ownership boundary.
Does this mean replicas necessarily accepted new writes after they were fenced?

No. The finding does not say that. It identifies delayed *pre-fence* replication replies as what enabled the later acknowledgment. The observed failure could not be described accurately as evidence that a replica newly accepted a write after fencing; that would add a fact the report does not provide.
But if the replies were from before the fence, why is the acknowledgment after promotion a problem?

The client-facing success came after promotion from the old leader, while the destination missed the write. The earlier origin of the replies does not make that later acknowledgment safe: it still has to fit the ownership transfer’s committed history. In the observed schedule, the destination did not account for the write that the old leader acknowledged.
Is it accurate to call this a lost acknowledged write?

You can say the destination missed a write that the old leader acknowledged after promotion. That states the observed failure precisely. Calling it permanently lost everywhere would go further than the finding, which does not describe every copy or any later recovery.
What does this tell us about treating the fence as the only important event?

The observed schedule shows why the leader’s ability to use in-flight replies matters as well as the fence event itself. Preventing fresh participation after a fence would not, on its own, explain what happens when replies associated with pre-fence replication arrive late and are used for a post-promotion acknowledgment. The finding exposes that timing issue; it does not specify a remedy.
Can I say the old leader formed a new quorum after promotion?

The report says delayed pre-fence replication replies let it acknowledge after promotion. It does not specify the leader’s exact quorum calculation or say that replicas formed a newly responding quorum after promotion. The narrower, supported claim is that those delayed replies sufficed for the old leader to issue the acknowledgment.
Is this merely a late response reaching the client for a write already acknowledged before promotion?

No—the stated finding is that the old leader **acknowledged after promotion** using delayed pre-fence replication replies. That differs from a response for an earlier acknowledgment merely arriving late. The distinction is central to why the schedule is problematic.
Do we know exactly when the write was first received or replicated?

No exact timeline is given beyond the relevant ordering: the replication replies were pre-fence, they were delayed, the old leader acknowledged after promotion, and the destination missed the write. We should not fill in the request’s arrival time or the precise sequence of replica actions.
Does the finding say whether a replica crashed in that particular schedule?

No. The fault-injection activity includes partitions and crashes, but this finding does not identify which faults occurred in the one reported schedule. We can describe the delayed-reply acknowledgment and missing destination write without attributing them to a particular crash or partition arrangement.
What should I make of the one-in-10,000 figure?

It is the observed count within the injected schedules: one schedule out of 10,000 exhibited this failure. The rarity in that set does not remove the safety concern, because the requirement is to preserve acknowledged writes and linearizability across the relevant failures. It also does not establish a general failure probability outside the tested schedules.
Would calling it an intermittent throughput issue be fair?

No. The reported problem is a safety issue: an old leader acknowledged after promotion, and the destination missed the write. The finding says nothing about throughput or the separate target of at least 80% of migration-free throughput under no failures and continuous writes.
Which of the two fault-injection checks does the schedule touch?

It touches both concerns named for that activity. The after-promotion acknowledgment is the stale-acknowledgment concern; the destination missing the acknowledged write is the write-survival concern at the ownership handoff. The report does not need to claim any additional observed failure to make those connections.
Should I say the destination missed every write acknowledged around cutover?
No. The evidence identifies **the write** acknowledged in the reported schedule. It does not say other writes were missed, or that all acknowledgments around promotion behaved the same way.
Could this be dismissed because the replication replies originated before the fence?

Not on that basis. The observed problem is precisely that replies associated with pre-fence replication could be used to acknowledge after promotion, while the destination missed the write. Their earlier origin is part of the failure mechanism, not a reason to disregard the later acknowledgment.
Does this observation tell us whether retry deduplication was involved?

No. The finding does not mention a client retry or deduplication. It identifies delayed replication replies, a post-promotion old-leader acknowledgment, and a write missing at the destination. Adding a retry to the explanation would be speculation.
What is the narrowest useful statement of the failure mode?

In 1/10,000 injected schedules, the old leader used delayed pre-fence replication replies to acknowledge a write after promotion, and the destination missed that write. That captures the observed ordering and consequence without assuming which replicas replied, which faults occurred in that schedule, or how the transfer might be changed.
Why is this still important if it appeared in only one injected schedule?

Because one observed execution is enough to demonstrate that this safety failure can occur in the tested setup. The count tells us how often it appeared among those 10,000 injected schedules, but the property at issue is whether an acknowledged write can be absent from the destination after promotion. In that one schedule, it was.

Here’s a hypothesis for handling delayed pre-fence acknowledgments: replay all writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs before promotion, including writes that are initially unacknowledged. That might preserve a write even if its pre-fence replication replies lead to an acknowledgment later.

The idea is to avoid limiting the handoff to writes already known to have been acknowledged when the logs are examined. If a write is present in the fenced old quorum’s logs and is replayed before promotion, the destination could retain it even if its acknowledgment is delayed. That is the preservation claim of the hypothesis, not an established result. It also does not, by itself, prevent the old leader from issuing an acknowledgment after promotion.
Why include initially unacknowledged writes? Isn’t the requirement specifically about acknowledged writes?

The requirement is to preserve acknowledged writes, but an acknowledgment may occur later than the replication activity associated with a write. A write that is initially unacknowledged could therefore become relevant to that requirement. The hypothesis proposes carrying every write found in those logs across before promotion, rather than deciding solely from its acknowledgment status at an earlier moment.
Does that mean the hypothesis treats every logged write as already committed?

No. Including a write in the replay set is not the same as asserting that it was committed or acknowledged when found. The hypothesis deliberately includes writes that were initially unacknowledged. Its claim is that replaying them may preserve a write if a delayed pre-fence acknowledgment occurs; it does not define the commitment status of every logged write.
What is important about looking at the fenced old quorum’s logs specifically?

That is the source of writes named in the hypothesis. It ties the replay set to the old quorum whose fence is involved in the transfer, rather than to whatever a single leader happens to remember. The claim still depends on what those logs contain and on the replay actually covering all writes found there; the hypothesis does not establish that every potentially acknowledged write must be present in that set.
Could I shorten the rule to replay only writes that already have an acknowledgment recorded?

That would change this hypothesis. It explicitly says to replay **all writes found** in the fenced old quorum’s logs, **even if initially unacknowledged**. The broader set is what makes the proposed treatment of delayed pre-fence acknowledgments possible.
Why must the replay happen before promotion?

The hypothesis places replay before the destination takes ownership so that the destination has the relevant logged writes when promotion occurs. If promotion happened first and replay were only attempted afterward, the hypothesis would not establish preservation at the ownership boundary. It does not specify a detailed replay-completion test or a promotion procedure.
Does copying those writes before promotion automatically make a late acknowledgment safe?

Not automatically. Having the write at the destination would address the risk that an acknowledged write is missing there. A late acknowledgment must also fit the rules for ownership and linearizable operations. This hypothesis is about preserving delayed pre-fence acknowledgments through replay; it is not, on its own, a complete account of when the old leader is permitted to acknowledge.
So there are really two different questions: whether the destination has the write and whether the old leader can still acknowledge it?

Yes. Replaying the writes found in the fenced quorum’s logs is proposed as an answer to the **preservation** question. It does not itself answer the **authority** question. Keeping those distinct prevents a write’s presence at the destination from being mistaken for permission for the old leader to issue a post-promotion acknowledgment.
If a write was never acknowledged, what does replaying it mean for the client?

The hypothesis does not assign a client-visible outcome to every initially unacknowledged write. Its replay set is intentionally broader than the set known to be acknowledged at that point. Whether such a write later counts as committed, is acknowledged, or is handled on a retry would require rules beyond this hypothesis.
Does “all writes found” imply replaying every write ever attempted on the old side?

No. The scope is specifically writes **found in the fenced old quorum’s logs**. An attempted write that is not found there is not included by that wording. Nor does the wording prove that the logs contain every attempted write or every write that could matter; those would be questions for evaluating the hypothesis.
Would replaying a write twice undermine the idea?

The hypothesis does not specify replay semantics, so it does not establish what repeated replay would do. A complete design would need to preserve a coherent operation history, including where retries or repeated transfer actions occur. We should not infer a particular deduplication mechanism—or assume repeated application is harmless—from the replay proposal alone.
What would have to be true for the preservation argument to work?

At minimum, the writes relevant to a delayed pre-fence acknowledgment would need to be among those found in the fenced old quorum’s logs, and the replay before promotion would need to leave the destination retaining them. The hypothesis states the proposed relationship; it has not demonstrated those conditions or specified how they are enforced.
Does the phrase “initially unacknowledged” mean we have decided those writes will eventually be acknowledged?

No. It describes their status at an initial point, not a prediction about every write’s eventual outcome. Some might never be acknowledged. The hypothesis includes them because it aims to cover the possibility of delayed pre-fence acknowledgments without assuming acknowledgment status is already settled when replay is selected.
Is the proposed replay a substitute for reconciling committed writes?

It is not enough to declare that from this hypothesis. Replaying all writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs describes a deliberately broad transfer set; determining which writes are committed and how they appear in the destination’s operation history remains a separate question. The hypothesis does not provide those rules or say that replay alone resolves them.
Does it guarantee survival through one replica crash?

No guarantee is established here. The hypothesis says replaying the specified logged writes before promotion preserves delayed pre-fence acknowledgments. To substantiate survival through a replica crash, a design would also have to make clear that the relevant logs and replayed writes remain available despite that crash. Those details and a validating result are not part of this hypothesis.
And can I claim it handles every partition arrangement?

Not yet. The proposed replay addresses a particular timing concern, but the hypothesis does not establish that every partition permits the required log information to be obtained or the replay to finish. It also does not promise progress during a partition. Its preservation claim needs evaluation under the relevant failure conditions.
Would this change the no-failure throughput target?

The performance requirement remains at least 80% of migration-free throughput while migrating a shard under continuous writes without failures. Replaying all writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs could affect the amount of transfer work, but the hypothesis gives no measurement or conclusion about that target.
How can I state the hypothesis without making it sound proven?

You could say: “Replaying all writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs before promotion, including initially unacknowledged writes, may preserve writes whose pre-fence replication replies lead to delayed acknowledgments.” That keeps the proposed mechanism and its intended benefit clear while leaving its correctness and broader cutover implications open.
How can cutover preserve writes acknowledged through delayed pre-fence replication replies after the source quorum is fenced?

The key is not to treat fencing as though it erases replication work already in flight. A reply generated before the fence may arrive afterward and may affect what the old leader believes it can acknowledge. Cutover therefore has to account for any write that could receive such an acknowledgment: either the destination must preserve that write before promotion, or the acknowledgment rules must prevent the old leader from issuing that later success. Which condition the protocol enforces needs to be made explicit.
Why can’t we decide what to transfer by looking only at writes already acknowledged when fencing finishes?

Because acknowledgment status at that instant may not capture replies still in transit. A write might be initially unacknowledged yet later be acknowledged using pre-fence replication replies. If cutover excludes it solely because no acknowledgment was visible when the fence finished, the destination could lack a write subsequently reported as successful.
Does that mean an in-flight reply gives the source permission to acknowledge after promotion?

No. The existence of a reply and the authority to issue a client-facing success are separate questions. The cutover rules must say whether a reply from pre-fence work can still count toward an acknowledgment after promotion. If the rules allow that acknowledgment, preservation must cover the write; if they disallow it, the source must actually enforce that restriction even while partitioned.
So what is the preservation question, stated as narrowly as possible?

For every write the old leader can acknowledge using delayed pre-fence replies, will the destination retain that write as part of the ownership handoff? The difficult case is a write not yet known to be acknowledged when transfer decisions are made, but acknowledged later. The answer cannot rest only on when a reply arrives.
Would looking in the fenced old quorum’s logs help identify those writes?

That is a way to frame the proposed replay approach: include writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs even if they are initially unacknowledged. Its intended purpose is to cover writes whose acknowledgment status may change when delayed replies arrive. To know whether it fully answers the question, we would still need to establish that every write capable of such a later acknowledgment is included and retained by the destination before promotion.
Why say “before promotion” rather than simply requiring that the destination eventually receives the write?

Because promotion is when the destination takes ownership. If the old leader can acknowledge a write after that point, a promise to transfer it eventually does not ensure the destination’s history accounts for that success at the boundary. The relevant requirement is preservation through the cutover, not merely a later opportunity to repair a missing write.
Does replaying an initially unacknowledged write mean telling the client it succeeded?

No. Transferring a write so that it cannot be lost if acknowledgment occurs is distinct from sending an acknowledgment or deciding that every transferred write committed. The protocol needs to keep those meanings separate. The question here is how to avoid omitting a write that *can* be acknowledged later, not whether all initially unacknowledged writes should succeed.
What if some logged writes never receive delayed replies?

Then their inclusion in a proposed replay set would be broader than the set of writes that ultimately get acknowledged. That breadth is the point of considering initially unacknowledged writes, but it creates a separate need to define their status at the destination. We cannot infer from their presence in a log alone that the client received success or that the write must be presented as committed.
I’m still unsure how a fenced quorum can be involved in a later acknowledgment. Isn’t it supposed to stop participating?

Stopping future participation does not necessarily retract replies already generated. The question specifically concerns *delayed pre-fence* replication replies: they can reach the leader after the fence without any replica taking a new post-fence action. Cutover has to define whether the leader may use those replies and, if it may, how the destination preserves the resulting acknowledged write.
Would it be enough to say that any acknowledgment issued after promotion is forbidden?

That would be one possible authority rule, but saying it is forbidden is not the same as enforcing it. A partitioned source may not learn promptly that promotion occurred. If the protocol relies on prohibiting such acknowledgments, its rules must make the prohibition effective despite that lack of notice. The preservation question remains important wherever delayed replies can still lead to a valid acknowledgment.
Could we avoid choosing between those approaches just by assuming the leader learns about the fence promptly?

No. The question matters precisely when replies and ownership information arrive at different times. A network partition can prevent prompt notice to the leader while leaving other messages or clients in play. A safe cutover cannot rely on the leader having the same immediate view of the fence and promotion as the destination.
How should committed-log reconciliation treat a write that is present before fencing but unacknowledged at that point?

It must not classify the write solely from the absence of an acknowledgment at that moment if delayed pre-fence replies could later support one. At the same time, presence alone does not establish that it was committed. The reconciliation and acknowledgment rules need a consistent account of that uncertainty so a later success cannot refer to a write the destination omitted.
Is this only a data-copy problem, then?

No. It joins a data question to an authority question. The data question is whether the destination retains every write that can still be acknowledged. The authority question is whether, and until when, the old leader may turn pre-fence replies into a success response. Solving only one leaves an ambiguity at promotion.
What does the client’s view add to the reasoning?

A client that receives a successful acknowledgment is entitled to have that write remain accounted for. The client cannot be expected to know that the leader used replies generated before fencing or delivered after it. Cutover must produce a consistent outcome regardless of that internal timing.
And if the client retries because it never receives the acknowledgment?

The missing response leaves the client uncertain about whether the write took effect. If the earlier attempt was committed, the destination must not behave as though it never existed; a retry also has to be handled consistently with that outcome. The present question does not specify the retry mechanism, but delayed acknowledgments make the boundary between an uncertain response and a committed write especially important.
How does one replica crash affect what it means to preserve a write through this boundary?

The preservation condition must remain true within the stated one-replica-crash scope. Merely identifying a potentially acknowledged write is not enough if the destination’s retained history can then lose it when a replica crashes. The question does not specify how logs or replay survive that crash, so it is a condition to establish rather than a guarantee we can assume.
Can a late reply be treated as harmless just because the write was replicated before the fence?

Not without checking both its acknowledgment status and its presence in the destination’s preserved history. “Pre-fence” describes the replication reply’s origin; it does not, by itself, settle whether a later client-facing acknowledgment is authorized or whether the destination has the write. Those are exactly the cutover questions the delayed reply raises.
What would be a precise way to ask whether a proposed cutover rule handles this?

Ask whether there can be an execution in which pre-fence replies arrive late, the old leader acknowledges a write after the source quorum is fenced, and the destination has been promoted without retaining that write. A satisfactory rule must exclude that combination—by constraining the acknowledgment, preserving the write before promotion, or establishing both conditions where needed.
So the fence and reconciliation have to agree on what can still become acknowledged?

Yes. The fence defines the boundary on old-side authority, while reconciliation determines what history the destination carries. For delayed pre-fence replies, those boundaries must agree: no write may become an acknowledged success under the cutover rules while being absent from the destination’s preserved history. The question remains how to specify and enforce that agreement.
I propose transferring shard ownership through joint consensus with quorum-intersecting log barriers. Alongside that, rate-limit snapshot streaming and persist request-ID deduplication.

That proposal addresses several parts of online migration together. Joint consensus and quorum-intersecting log barriers are meant to connect the ownership change to the shard’s log history. Rate limiting addresses the resource cost of snapshot streaming while writes continue, and persistent request-ID deduplication addresses retries across the handoff and a replica crash. Those are proposed components, not yet a demonstrated safety or throughput result.
What does joint consensus contribute to an ownership transfer?

Conceptually, it makes the transition between the old and destination configurations a coordinated agreement rather than an isolated declaration by either side. The intended benefit is that the authority to commit operations cannot split into incompatible old and new histories. The proposal does not specify the membership-change rules or exactly when either configuration may acknowledge an operation, so that benefit still needs a precise protocol argument.
And what is a quorum-intersecting log barrier meant to protect?

It is meant to make the ownership boundary depend on log information shared across the relevant quorums. If a write can be acknowledged on one side of the handoff, the barrier should prevent promotion of a history that simply omits it. “Quorum-intersecting” points to a structural requirement: the quorums involved in establishing the boundary cannot be disjoint in a way that permits conflicting committed histories. The proposal does not define the barrier’s exact contents or completion condition.
Could I just say that any majority intersects any other majority?

Only after specifying which configurations and quorum rules you mean. Two majorities of the same fixed membership intersect, but an ownership transfer can involve different memberships. The proposal specifically calls for quorum-intersecting log barriers together with joint consensus; the necessary intersection across the transition has to follow from the actual rules, not from the word “majority” alone.
Does a log barrier copy the entire shard?

Not necessarily. The proposal distinguishes log barriers from snapshot streaming. The barrier concerns the log history and the authority boundary, while the snapshot stream concerns transferring shard state. Nothing here specifies how much state either carries, or implies that one replaces the other.
If writes keep arriving during the snapshot stream, can the destination rely on the snapshot alone?

A snapshot alone does not explain what happens to operations after the state it captures. With continuous writes, the ownership-transfer rules must ensure the destination has the history needed for linearizable operations and preservation of acknowledged writes. The proposed joint consensus and log barriers are directed at that boundary, but the proposal does not spell out the complete data-transfer sequence.
What would make an acknowledgment at the old side safe while the transfer is underway?

It would have to be compatible with the history and authority that the destination will inherit. In particular, an acknowledged write cannot disappear from the destination’s account of the shard, and two sides cannot acknowledge incompatible operations independently. The proposed joint-consensus and barrier rules need to establish those conditions; naming them does not itself say when the old side may acknowledge.
Does this proposal rely on every replica learning of the ownership change at the same time?

It should not have to, given the requirement to preserve safety across network partitions. A replica or client can have stale information. The important question is whether the agreement and acknowledgment rules still prevent an incompatible success when communication is disrupted. The proposal does not promise that all requests remain available during a partition.
What would I need to check about the log barrier if a replication reply arrives late?

Check whether a write that can still become acknowledged through an in-flight reply is included in the history protected by the ownership boundary, or whether the acknowledgment rules make that later success impossible. The log barrier and joint-consensus rules must agree on what can count as an acknowledged write. This is a question for the proposed rules, not a claim that they already handle every timing case.
Why persist request-ID deduplication rather than keep it only in memory?

A retry may cross the ownership change, and one replica may crash. If the information used to recognize an earlier request disappears with volatile state, a retry could be handled without regard to the earlier outcome. Persisting request-ID deduplication is intended to retain that recognition across the handoff and failure. The proposal does not specify request-ID generation, retention time, or storage format.
Does a request ID tell us whether an earlier attempt committed?

An ID lets the system recognize that two attempts correspond to the same request; it does not, by itself, establish the earlier attempt’s outcome. The persisted deduplication information must be consistent with the committed history and with what was acknowledged. The proposal names the persistence requirement but does not define the records or lookup rules.
Suppose the client retries at the destination after getting no response from the old side. What must stay consistent?

The destination must not treat the retry in a way that contradicts what actually happened to the original attempt. If that attempt committed, its effect and the retry’s outcome must be consistent with one linearizable history; if it did not, the retry still has to follow the current ownership rules. Persistent request-ID deduplication is proposed to help manage that distinction, without assuming a missing response means the original failed.
Does storing deduplication information on one replica meet the crash requirement?

The proposal does not identify where or how that information is persisted, so it would be premature to say. To satisfy the one-replica-crash requirement, the information needed to handle retries consistently must remain available when a replica crashes. Persistence is the proposed property; the durability and transfer conditions still need to be specified.
Where does rate limiting fit if safety depends on finishing the transfer?

Rate limiting controls how aggressively snapshot streaming consumes resources while ordinary operations continue. It must be considered alongside the need for migration to make progress; an extremely restrictive limit might leave the transfer unable to catch up under continuous writes. The proposal gives no rate, scheduling policy, or completion measurement.
Can I infer that rate-limited streaming will meet the throughput requirement?

No. The target is at least 80% of migration-free throughput, without failures, while migrating a shard under continuous writes. Rate limiting is a proposed way to reduce interference with normal traffic, but no throughput result is given. Both the target and the continuous-write condition would have to be reflected in any performance assessment.
Is the 80% comparison against migration-free throughput, rather than against a different migration method?

Yes. The stated baseline is throughput without migration. During migration of a shard under continuous writes and without failures, throughput must remain at least 80% of that baseline. The proposal does not provide a number for either measured throughput or the effect of joint consensus, barriers, deduplication, and streaming.
Could joint consensus be treated as a substitute for retaining acknowledged writes at the destination?

No. Agreement on ownership must be tied to the log history the new owner carries. A transfer could have a clear authority boundary yet still fail the goal if an acknowledged write were missing. The quorum-intersecting log barriers are proposed to connect those concerns; the actual rules would need to show that the connection holds.
And could persistent deduplication substitute for the log barriers?

No. Deduplication concerns recognizing repeated client requests and preserving their outcomes consistently. A log barrier concerns the committed history and ownership boundary. Each addresses a different source of inconsistency, and neither name alone supplies a complete proof of linearizability or crash-safe transfer.
How should I characterize the proposal without presenting it as a validated design?

Propose joint consensus with quorum-intersecting log barriers for ownership transfer, rate-limited snapshot streaming for the online data movement, and persistent request-ID deduplication for retries. Then state the obligations separately: preserve linearizability and acknowledged writes across retries, partitions, and one replica crash, and sustain at least 80% of migration-free throughput under continuous writes without failures. The proposal identifies an approach to those obligations; it does not report that they have been met.

I plan to implement joint-consensus log barriers and durable request-ID deduplication, then fault-inject partitions and crashes. I also want to benchmark throttled streaming against the requirement to sustain at least 80% of migration-free throughput while migrating a shard under continuous writes without failures.

That plan has two distinct evaluation tracks. The fault injection is for the safety obligations: linearizable operations and preservation of acknowledged writes across retries, network partitions, and one replica crash. The benchmark is for the no-failure performance comparison during migration under continuous writes. Implementing the barriers and deduplication, running the injections, and measuring throughput are planned work; the plan does not report their outcomes.
What should the joint-consensus log barriers accomplish in the implementation?

They are intended to connect the change in ownership to the log history that the destination must carry. The critical property to establish is that an ownership change cannot leave an acknowledged write outside the destination’s preserved history or allow incompatible acknowledgments from the old and new sides. The plan does not specify the barrier’s exact rule, so that remains an implementation and validation obligation.
Is a log barrier simply a marker saying that migration is complete?

Calling it a marker would not, by itself, establish anything about writes or authority. For this plan, the meaningful question is what the joint-consensus log barrier requires before ownership can change and how that requirement remains effective when messages are delayed or a participant is partitioned. Its precise representation is not stated.
How does durable request-ID deduplication fit into the same work?

A client can retry without knowing whether an earlier attempt took effect. Request-ID deduplication is intended to let the store recognize that relationship across the transfer, while durability keeps the information from depending solely on transient state. Its recorded outcome must remain consistent with the log history and with any acknowledgment given to the client. The plan does not choose a storage format or retention policy.
If a request has an ID, can I assume retry handling is solved?

No. An ID identifies a repeated request; it does not itself tell the destination whether the first attempt committed or what response, if any, was valid. The implementation must tie durable deduplication to the operation’s actual outcome. Fault injection can then examine whether retries remain consistent during partitions and crashes, but no result is given yet.
What should the partition injection challenge specifically?

It should challenge any assumption that all participants learn about the ownership change promptly. A source with stale information might still receive requests, while the destination has a different view. The safety question is whether the implemented log barriers and acknowledgment rules prevent incompatible successes despite that separation—not whether every request stays available during a partition.
And what is the crash scope I should keep in mind?

The goal requires preservation of linearizability and acknowledged writes through **one replica crash**. The plan says to inject crashes, but does not specify their schedules or identify which replica fails. When interpreting the work, keep the stated one-crash requirement distinct from any broader claim about multiple crashes.
Could the fault injection focus only on whether ownership eventually reaches the destination?

That would not cover the stated safety obligations. A transfer could eventually complete yet acknowledge conflicting operations or omit an earlier acknowledged write. The injections need to make those outcomes observable in the implemented behavior; progress to the destination alone is not a substitute for checking operation history and write survival.
What would count as a relevant retry failure during a partition?

For example, a retry must not cause the system to contradict an outcome already committed for that same request, nor may an acknowledged write disappear because the retry reaches a different owner. That is a general statement of the property to test, not a reported failure or a claim that a particular retry schedule has been selected.
How should I separate the benchmark from the fault-injection work?

The benchmark targets the specified **without-failures** condition: a shard is migrating under continuous writes, with throttled streaming, and throughput is compared with migration-free throughput. Partition and crash injection targets safety under failures. A safety result would not measure throughput, and a no-failure throughput result would not establish safety across partitions or a replica crash.
What exactly does the 80% figure mean in that benchmark?

Throughput while the shard is migrating under continuous writes must be **at least 80% of migration-free throughput**, without failures. It is a relative lower bound against the no-migration baseline, not a target relative to an unthrottled migration run. The plan contains no measured baseline or migration throughput yet.
Could I benchmark after writes stop and still say I tested the target?
No. The target explicitly applies while migrating a shard **under continuous writes**. Measuring an idle shard, or measuring only after migration finishes, would not by itself test that condition.
Why throttle streaming if it might take longer to finish migration?

Throttling is intended to limit the resources consumed by streaming while ordinary writes continue. There is a balance to evaluate: limiting streaming may protect throughput, but migration still has to make progress under the workload. The plan does not provide a throttle setting, a completion-time target, or a measured tradeoff.

How much can I conclude about migration completion from the catch-up observation?

You can say the bursty and Zipf runs completed log catch-up. That does not, by itself, report when destination promotion occurred, how long cutover took, or whether every step of migration completed. Those would be separate outcomes.
Can the reported throughput and catch-up outcomes settle the safety requirements too?

No. This decision concerns prioritization and adaptive transfer egress, supported by throughput and catch-up observations. Linearizability and preservation of acknowledged writes across retries, partitions, and one replica crash remain distinct safety requirements; performance and catch-up results are not substitutes for them.
Is this a universal throughput guarantee for all continuous-write workloads?

No. The decision adopts the policy because the reported bursty and Zipf runs exceeded 80% and completed catch-up. That is evidence under those run conditions, not a stated guarantee for every workload, replica configuration, or operating condition.
Does the decision give an exact catch-up duration or cutover latency?
No. It says catch-up completed in the bursty and Zipf runs, but gives no catch-up duration or cutover-latency value. The completion observation should not be turned into a timing measurement.
Would a fixed 20% egress limit describe the chosen policy accurately?

No. The chosen policy includes an adaptive reduction from 20% to 10% at an 86%-of-baseline throughput trigger, alongside foreground-write priority. A fixed 20% cap omits the adaptive part of the decision.
Can you state the decision and its supporting observation in one sentence?

Adopt foreground-write priority and reduce transfer egress from 20% to 10% of replica egress at an 86%-of-migration-free-throughput trigger; the reported bursty and Zipf runs exceeded the 80% throughput target and completed log catch-up.

I propose staging the destination replicas as Raft learners using copy-on-write snapshots. After they catch up to a barrier index and the deduplication state has been replicated, we would jointly reconfigure ownership.

That is a proposed sequence for online shard migration. The destination replicas first receive state as Raft learners, with copy-on-write snapshots providing a view to transfer while foreground operations continue. Joint reconfiguration waits for two prerequisites: barrier-index catch-up and replication of deduplication state. The proposal does not yet establish that those steps preserve linearizability and acknowledged writes under failures, or that migration sustains the required throughput.
Why stage the destination as learners instead of immediately treating those replicas as owners?

Staging separates receiving the shard’s state from taking part in the ownership change. In the proposed sequence, the destination replicas have an opportunity to catch up before joint reconfiguration gives the new configuration authority. The exact privileges of a learner and the rules for changing membership would have to be specified in the Raft design; the proposal does not define them.
Does a learner receiving a snapshot mean it is ready to serve linearizable operations?

No. A snapshot gives it a starting view of the shard, but writes may continue after the snapshot’s point in the history. The proposal specifically requires catch-up to a barrier index and replication of deduplication state before joint reconfiguration. Snapshot receipt alone is not presented as a condition for taking ownership.
What does copy-on-write contribute while writes are still arriving?

Conceptually, copy-on-write lets a snapshot retain a view of state while subsequent writes continue to change the active state. That makes it a plausible way to stage data without requiring the shard to be idle for the entire copy. The proposal does not specify its storage implementation, resource cost, or measured effect on foreground throughput.
Could I say the copy-on-write snapshot includes every write made during migration?

No. A snapshot represents a view at a particular point; continuous writes can occur afterward. Catch-up is a separate part of the proposal precisely because staging a snapshot does not, by itself, account for every later change. The proposal does not spell out the mechanism that brings learners from that snapshot view to the barrier index.
What is the barrier index supposed to identify?

It identifies a point in the shard’s ordered history that the destination replicas are to catch up to before joint reconfiguration. That gives the ownership transition a stated history boundary rather than relying on the vague claim that the snapshot is ‘recent enough.’ The proposal does not specify how the index is chosen, recorded, or checked.
If writes remain continuous, wouldn’t the latest log position keep moving?

Yes; continuous writes make ‘caught up with everything forever’ an unsuitable condition. Catch-up to a barrier index refers to a defined point, even though additional operations may arrive afterward. A complete protocol would still need to account for those later operations through the authority transition. The proposal does not say that reaching the barrier index alone resolves all post-barrier writes.
Does a learner merely knowing the barrier-index number count as catching up?

No. Knowing the number and having the necessary shard history through that point are different. The proposed prerequisite is *barrier-index catch-up*, not receipt of a notification containing an index. What evidence is required to declare that catch-up complete remains unspecified.
Why replicate deduplication state before joint reconfiguration?

A client can retry across an ownership change without knowing whether its earlier attempt took effect. The destination needs the information required to recognize and handle such a retry consistently with the established outcome. Replicating deduplication state before joint reconfiguration is intended to keep that information from being stranded on the old side when authority changes. The proposal does not define the representation or retention of that state.
Is deduplication state simply another name for the shard’s key-value data?

No. The key-value state records the shard’s data; deduplication state concerns identifying repeated requests and their relevant outcomes. A destination might have the data needed to answer a read yet still lack information for handling a retry consistently. The proposal names deduplication-state replication separately from snapshot staging and barrier-index catch-up for that reason.
If the retry has a request ID, doesn’t that settle whether the earlier attempt succeeded?

A request ID can identify the retry as another attempt of the same request, but the ID alone does not reveal what happened to the earlier attempt. The replicated deduplication state has to be consistent with the operation history and any acknowledgment the client received. The proposal does not specify which outcomes it records or how it keeps them aligned with the barrier.
Are catch-up and deduplication-state replication alternative ways of preparing the destination?

No. The proposal requires *both* before joint reconfiguration. Barrier-index catch-up addresses the ordered shard history the learners need. Deduplication-state replication addresses information needed to treat requests repeated across the handoff consistently. Completing only one would leave the other prerequisite unsatisfied.
Does the proposal say which of those two prerequisites has to finish first?

It does not specify an order between them. The ordering it does state is that joint reconfiguration occurs **after** barrier-index catch-up **and** deduplication-state replication. Their internal sequencing or possible overlap is left open.
What should joint reconfiguration accomplish once those prerequisites are met?

It should change the configuration’s authority in a coordinated way, rather than treating state transfer alone as an ownership grant. To meet the migration goal, operations across that change must remain linearizable, and acknowledged writes must survive. The proposal identifies joint reconfiguration as the ownership-transfer step, but does not give its exact quorum rules or prove those properties.
Could a partitioned replica still think the old configuration owns the shard?

It could have stale information. The safety question is not merely what it believes, but whether the reconfiguration and acknowledgment rules let it successfully acknowledge a write that conflicts with the new ownership history. The proposal must ultimately remain safe across network partitions; it does not specify how an isolated participant learns of the change or whether every request remains available during a partition.
Where does the one-replica-crash requirement enter this design?

The snapshot state, history through the barrier, deduplication information, and ownership change all need to remain consistent if one replica crashes. Staging learners and replicating deduplication state are relevant pieces, but their names alone do not establish what survives a crash or when promotion is safe. The goal is preservation of linearizability and acknowledged writes within that one-crash scope, not a stated guarantee for more crashes.
Suppose a write is acknowledged before reconfiguration, but its effect is not in the initial snapshot. What does this proposal require?

The write cannot be omitted from the authoritative history just because it arrived after the snapshot’s view. Barrier-index catch-up is intended to account for the ordered history through its boundary, while the reconfiguration rules must handle operations around and after that boundary consistently. Whether a particular acknowledged write is covered depends on the precise relationship among its commitment, the barrier, and reconfiguration; those rules are not yet stated.
Would completing log catch-up automatically establish that retries are safe?

No. Catch-up and request deduplication address related but distinct information. Even if the destination has the shard’s ordered changes through the barrier, a client retry crossing the ownership boundary still needs to be associated with its earlier attempt’s outcome. That is why deduplication-state replication is a separate prerequisite in the proposal.
Is the aim to pause all writes until joint reconfiguration finishes?

The proposal does not prescribe a write pause. It is framed as online migration, with copy-on-write snapshot staging and learner catch-up while operations may continue. There might be coordination around the ownership boundary, but neither a blanket pause nor a promise that no request ever waits is specified.
How does this relate to the throughput requirement during continuous writes?

The no-failure requirement is to sustain at least **80% of migration-free throughput** while migrating a shard under continuous writes. Snapshot creation and transfer, learner catch-up, deduplication-state replication, and joint reconfiguration could all affect operation throughput. This proposal provides an approach to staging and handoff, not a measurement showing that its full migration path reaches the threshold.
Can I infer a particular transfer throttle or catch-up time from the copy-on-write and learner choices?

No. Neither a transfer cap nor a catch-up time is stated in this proposal. Copy-on-write snapshots and learner staging describe how the destination is prepared; they do not specify the resources used, the duration of catch-up, or a throughput result.
What should I be careful not to claim when describing this as a design?

Do not equate staging a learner with promoting an owner, receipt of a snapshot with barrier-index catch-up, or possession of shard data with possession of deduplication state. Also avoid claiming that joint reconfiguration has already been shown to handle every retry, partition, and one-replica-crash execution. Those are correctness obligations for the proposed sequence, not results supplied with it.
Can you state the proposal and its open obligations concisely?

Stage destination replicas as Raft learners using copy-on-write snapshots; once they have caught up to a barrier index and deduplication state has been replicated, jointly reconfigure ownership. The proposal still needs precise rules and evidence for linearizability and acknowledged-write survival across retries, partitions, and one replica crash, as well as the no-failure target of at least 80% of migration-free throughput under continuous writes.
How can destination replicas catch up with continuous writes without disrupting source-quorum acknowledgments before cutover?

The distinction to preserve is between preparing the destination and changing who can acknowledge writes. In the proposed sequence, destination replicas are staged as Raft learners: they can receive a copy-on-write snapshot and catch up toward a barrier index while the source configuration continues to handle writes. Before cutover, learner progress should not become an unstated prerequisite for each source-quorum acknowledgment. Whether the destination can catch up quickly enough without competing excessively with foreground writes is a separate question the proposal has not answered.
Does staging them as learners mean writes stop while the snapshot is created?

Not as stated. The copy-on-write snapshot is proposed to provide a view of the shard while writes continue. It does not include every subsequent write, so the learners still need to catch up. The proposal does not promise that snapshot creation has no cost or that no individual request ever waits.
If the source continues acknowledging writes, won’t the destination always be behind?

It may be behind the latest write at any particular moment. Catch-up to a barrier index is a more specific condition than being current with an indefinitely moving latest position. The question is whether the destination can acquire the required history through that defined boundary while new writes continue, and how the ownership transition accounts for writes beyond it. Neither the rate of convergence nor those precise boundary rules are specified here.
Why is the barrier index useful if the source can acknowledge more writes after that index?

It gives the destination a definite history point to reach rather than an ambiguous instruction to be fully caught up. But reaching that point alone does not settle the status of later writes. The eventual joint reconfiguration must keep acknowledgments around the boundary consistent with the history the new configuration retains. A barrier is useful only as part of that larger ownership rule.
Should source acknowledgments wait for every learner to apply each write before cutover?

That is not a requirement of the learner-staging proposal. Making every pre-cutover source acknowledgment depend on destination catch-up would couple normal write completion to the migration stream, potentially disrupting source-quorum acknowledgments. At the same time, leaving learners out of the acknowledgment path does not excuse losing any write that the source does acknowledge; the transfer and reconfiguration rules must still preserve it.
Is the idea that the source quorum keeps its usual authority until joint reconfiguration?

At a conceptual level, the question asks how to keep pre-cutover source-quorum acknowledgments working while destination learners prepare. Exactly when that authority changes has to be specified by the joint-reconfiguration protocol. Learners receiving data must not silently be treated as owners, and preparation alone must not create a second independent acknowledgment authority.
What can the learners do without being part of the source quorum?

They can be prepared for the transition by receiving snapshot state, catching up toward the barrier index, and receiving the deduplication state named in the proposal. That separates destination preparation from the source’s pre-cutover acknowledgment decision. The proposal does not specify the individual transfer messages or precisely how learner progress is confirmed.
Does the snapshot itself tell the learners which writes the source acknowledged?

Not necessarily. It represents a view at a point in the shard’s history; writes can continue afterward, and acknowledgment information around the handoff needs a consistent history boundary. The destination’s catch-up and the eventual reconfiguration have to account for acknowledged writes that are not contained in the snapshot view. Snapshot receipt by itself is not evidence that the learners have all such writes.
How do I avoid making the catch-up traffic interfere with the source quorum’s write traffic?

The design needs to account for competition between migration transfer and foreground writes. Controlling transfer egress and giving foreground writes priority are ways to frame that resource question, but neither a cap nor a priority label automatically proves that acknowledgments remain timely. In particular, the question asks for a way to prepare learners without making the source’s pre-cutover quorum acknowledgment wait on their receipt of each update; the actual scheduling and measured impact are separate details.
If I limit transfer traffic, could that prevent catch-up altogether?

It could affect whether the learners make sufficient progress while writes keep arriving. That is why throughput and catch-up are distinct concerns: protecting foreground work does not by itself show that the destination reaches the barrier. No transfer rate, incoming write rate, or completion bound is specified in this question, so we cannot conclude whether a particular limit permits catch-up.
Could we just declare the learners caught up whenever the snapshot transfer finishes?

No. Snapshot completion and barrier-index catch-up are different conditions in the proposal. Continuous writes may have changed the shard after the snapshot’s view. Declaring catch-up solely because the snapshot arrived would leave those changes unaccounted for.
What should be true of a write that the source quorum acknowledges while a learner is behind?

It must remain part of the history preserved through ownership transfer. The learner’s temporary lag need not, by itself, prevent a source-quorum acknowledgment before cutover, but promotion must not make that acknowledged write disappear. The precise protocol must connect the source’s acknowledgment history with what the destination retains when authority changes.
Does deduplication-state replication also have to finish before reconfiguration?

Yes, that is a separate prerequisite in the stated proposal: jointly reconfigure after both barrier-index catch-up and deduplication-state replication. The latter matters when a request is retried across the transition. It does not imply that the source should wait for the learners’ deduplication-state updates on every pre-cutover acknowledgment; the proposal leaves the exact replication and completion rules open.
Suppose a client retries at a learner before the ownership change. Can the learner acknowledge it?

Learner staging alone does not grant ownership or acknowledgment authority. A retry has to be handled consistently with whichever configuration is authorized and with the earlier attempt’s outcome. The proposal does not define how a client is routed while learners are catching up, so it would be unwarranted to claim a learner can acknowledge that request merely because it holds a snapshot or deduplication state.
What if a partition interrupts the learner transfer but the source quorum can still acknowledge writes?

The source’s ability to make safe progress and the learners’ ability to catch up can diverge. If the transfer cannot establish its prerequisites, the design should not infer that joint reconfiguration is ready merely because source acknowledgments continue. Conversely, migration need not force a source-quorum acknowledgment to depend on a partitioned learner before cutover. Exact availability in a partition is not promised by the goal; linearizability and acknowledged-write survival remain required.
Would one replica crash change what it means for the learners to be ready?

Readiness must be defined so that the ownership transfer still preserves linearizability and acknowledged writes within the one-replica-crash scope. A snapshot or catch-up indication held only in state that disappears with that crash would not, by itself, establish that the destination retains the necessary history. The proposal does not specify its durability or readiness test, so that is a question to resolve rather than a property we can assume.
How should I distinguish source acknowledgment from destination readiness in one sentence?

Before cutover, the source’s authorized quorum can acknowledge writes under its applicable rules, while destination learners independently prepare the history and deduplication state required for joint reconfiguration. The two processes must eventually meet at a safe ownership boundary, but learner preparation should not be mistaken for either an acknowledgment quorum or an automatic promotion.
Is it enough to show that writes remain fast before cutover?

No. The question also asks whether the destination can catch up while writes continue. Fast source acknowledgments do not establish that learners reach the barrier, and successful catch-up does not establish that foreground throughput stays at least 80% of migration-free throughput. The broader goal requires safe transfer of acknowledged writes as well as the specified no-failure throughput during migration.
What is the central issue to verify for the proposed learner approach?

Verify that destination learners can reach the barrier index and receive deduplication state without being placed in the pre-cutover source-quorum acknowledgment path, while every write the source does acknowledge remains accounted for when joint reconfiguration changes ownership. That frames the needed safety and progress conditions without claiming that the proposal has already demonstrated them.
My hypothesis is that a copy-on-write snapshot plus throttled Raft learner replay can get the destination to a barrier index while the source quorum continues acknowledging writes.

That proposes a way to overlap destination catch-up with ongoing service. The copy-on-write snapshot gives the learners a starting view, and throttled replay advances them toward the barrier index as writes continue. Meanwhile, the source quorum continues acknowledging writes. This is a hypothesis about what those activities can achieve together, not a reported catch-up or throughput result.
Why do I need replay if I already have the copy-on-write snapshot?

The snapshot represents a view of the shard, but writes can continue after the view it captures. Learner replay is the proposed way to advance from that starting view toward the barrier index. Receiving the snapshot alone would not show that the learners have caught up to that index.
Does copy-on-write mean the source must stop writing to make a consistent snapshot?

The point of using a copy-on-write snapshot in this hypothesis is to obtain a snapshot view while writes continue. That does not claim snapshot creation has no overhead or that no request ever waits. The proposed overlap is what matters here: destination preparation and source-quorum acknowledgments proceed during the same migration period.
What does the barrier index add to the phrase “the learners catch up”?

It gives catch-up a defined point in the history. With continuous writes, the latest position can keep advancing, so saying only that the learners are “current” is ambiguous. The hypothesis is specifically that snapshot transfer and throttled replay get them to a barrier index; it does not define how that index is selected or verified.
If writes keep coming in after the barrier index, can the hypothesis still be true?

Yes. Reaching a specified barrier index does not mean that writes have stopped or that learners are forever at the latest position. The hypothesis says they can reach that particular index while the source quorum continues acknowledging writes. How later writes are handled at an eventual ownership change is a separate protocol question, not settled by reaching the barrier.
Is a learner’s receiving the barrier index number enough?

No. The proposed catch-up concerns the learner reaching the history through that index, not merely learning which number to aim for. The hypothesis does not provide the exact readiness test, so receiving a notification about the index should not be treated as proof of catch-up.
What role does throttling play if I also want the learners to catch up?

Throttling limits the replay’s resource use while the source quorum continues handling writes. The tension is that too little transfer progress could leave the learners behind the barrier, whereas more replay traffic could compete with foreground work. The hypothesis asserts that the proposed combination can reach the barrier without stopping source-quorum acknowledgments; it gives no throttle setting or evidence that a particular setting achieves that balance.
Does throttling imply a specific percentage of replica egress here?
No percentage is specified in this hypothesis. It says the Raft learner replay is throttled. We should not assign it a numerical cap or infer a measured throughput ratio from that description.
Could the source quorum acknowledge each write without waiting for the learners?

That is the separation the hypothesis is exploring: source-quorum acknowledgments continue while the destination learners catch up through replay. It does not prescribe the precise acknowledgment rules or claim that a learner’s receipt of every write is required before the source can respond. Any eventual cutover would still have to preserve the acknowledged history.
If learners are not part of those acknowledgments, does their lag make source acknowledgments unsafe?

Lag alone does not establish that a pre-cutover source-quorum acknowledgment is unsafe. The issue is whether acknowledged writes remain accounted for when ownership eventually changes. This hypothesis addresses reaching a barrier while acknowledgments continue; it does not, by itself, prove the safety of a later reconfiguration.
Could the snapshot finish but the replay never reach the barrier under continuous writes?

That is a possibility the hypothesis has to be evaluated against. Completing the snapshot and reaching the barrier are different events. Without information about replay progress relative to continuing writes, we cannot conclude from the proposed mechanism alone that the barrier will be reached.
Does reaching the barrier establish that migration is complete?

No. Barrier-index catch-up is the destination-preparation outcome named in the hypothesis. Ownership transfer and the treatment of operations around that transition require their own rules. The hypothesis does not state that reaching the barrier automatically promotes the learners or completes migration.
Is deduplication-state replication included in this claim?

Not in the stated hypothesis. It concerns a copy-on-write snapshot, throttled Raft learner replay, reaching a barrier index, and continued source-quorum acknowledgments. A broader transfer may also need retry-related state, but this particular claim does not say it has been replicated or that retries have been validated.
What if the source keeps acknowledging writes while the learners are replaying—what must I avoid inferring from that observation alone?

It would show one side of the proposed overlap, not both. Continued acknowledgments do not establish that the learners reached the barrier. Conversely, learners reaching the barrier would not alone show that source acknowledgments continued throughout catch-up. Both conditions belong to the hypothesis.
Does “continues acknowledging” guarantee a particular write throughput?

No. It describes continued successful acknowledgments, not a measured rate. In particular, it does not establish the separate goal of sustaining at least 80% of migration-free throughput without failures during migration under continuous writes. A throughput comparison would need its own evidence.
Does the hypothesis already account for a partition or one replica crash?

It does not specify a failure schedule or give a failure-case result. The stated claim is about destination catch-up through snapshot and throttled learner replay while source-quorum acknowledgments continue. Preserving linearizability and acknowledged writes across partitions and one replica crash remains an obligation of the broader migration design, not a conclusion from this hypothesis.
How could I state a direct test of this claim without presuming an outcome?

Observe migration under continuous writes and check both whether the destination learners reach the specified barrier index through the copy-on-write snapshot and throttled replay, and whether the source quorum continues acknowledging writes before cutover. The test would also need to identify what counts as reaching the barrier. That describes what to look for; it does not report that either condition has occurred.
So what is the precise hypothesis, with its limits kept visible?

A copy-on-write snapshot followed by throttled Raft learner replay can bring the destination replicas to a barrier index while the source quorum continues acknowledging writes under continuous writes. Whether it does so, how quickly it catches up, and what throughput or cutover guarantees follow are not established by the hypothesis itself.

That plan tests whether destination preparation can proceed alongside ongoing source service. What does the 86% trigger refer to here?

It is a throughput trigger, expressed relative to migration-free operation throughput. Why would I use a copy-on-write snapshot for the learners?

It provides a snapshot view that can be staged at the destination while the source continues to process writes. Because new writes can occur after the snapshot’s view, the snapshot alone is not the catch-up result. The learners must still advance through the relevant history to the barrier index.
Does implementing the snapshot mean source writes never pause?

Not by itself. Copy-on-write is intended to allow snapshot preparation to overlap with writes, but the plan does not measure whether individual requests wait or how much overhead snapshot work creates. That is one reason to observe source write acknowledgments while the destination prepares.
What exactly am I trying to establish by measuring barrier catch-up?

If writes keep arriving, is reaching a barrier index still meaningful?

Why measure source write acknowledgments separately from barrier catch-up?

What does 'source write acknowledgments' mean here—just that requests reached the source?

No. Receiving or attempting a write is different from acknowledging it to the client. The proposed measurement concerns source write acknowledgments while continuous writes are arriving. The plan does not specify the exact count, rate, or timing measure that will be used to report them.
Could I infer that normal write throughput is preserved if I see any acknowledgments during catch-up?

No. Continued acknowledgments show that writes can complete, but not at what rate relative to migration-free operation. Should a source-quorum acknowledgment wait for each learner to replay that write?

The question this plan investigates is whether learners can prepare without disrupting pre-cutover source-quorum acknowledgments. If the source acknowledges a write while learners lag, is that automatically a safety failure?

No. Learner lag during preparation is distinct from losing an acknowledged write during ownership transfer. Any later reconfiguration still has to preserve the source’s acknowledged history. The measurement plan focuses on reaching the barrier while acknowledgments continue; it does not, by itself, establish cutover safety.
Could throttling protect write acknowledgments yet prevent the learners from catching up?

Conversely, would fast barrier catch-up prove the throttle works well for writes?

Does the 86% trigger guarantee that the 80% throughput target is maintained?

Can I specify from this plan exactly how much learner traffic is allowed after the trigger fires?

Not from the wording of this plan alone. It calls for 86%-triggered learner throttling but does not state the resulting transfer cap, how throughput is sampled, or how quickly a change takes effect. Those details should not be inferred from the trigger value.
Are snapshot creation and learner replay both part of the observation period?

Does reaching the barrier mean the destination replicas are immediately owners?

Does the plan test whether deduplication state has been replicated?

What about partitions and one replica crash? Are they included in this measurement?

Could I report successful migration if the learners reach the barrier and source writes continue?

Could the learners receive the snapshot and still fail the catch-up check?

Yes. The snapshot provides a starting view, but writes may continue after it. The learners still need to advance to the barrier index. The activity measures that progress rather than treating snapshot completion as equivalent to catch-up.
Why is acknowledgment continuity separate from the throughput-trigger percentage?

The 86% trigger is a condition for changing transfer throttling. Acknowledgment continuity asks whether the source keeps issuing successful write acknowledgments while learner preparation proceeds. It would establish only one of the two observed conditions. Continuing source acknowledgments would not show that the destination becomes ready for reconfiguration. Does the 60-minute duration imply catch-up has to finish by the end?

It sets the observation window for the WriteHot-1 run. The activity checks barrier-index catch-up, but does not say whether it occurs within those 60 minutes. If it does not, the accurate report would be that catch-up was not observed within that window, not an invented completion time.
What if the 86% trigger never fires during the run?

The run would still exercise the configured throttling policy and could still yield catch-up and acknowledgment observations. But it would not demonstrate how the policy behaves after a trigger event. The activity gives no switching trace, so we cannot say whether the trigger fires.
Could I infer the cap changes from 20% to 10% in this run?

The activity specifies 86%-triggered throttling, but does not report an actual cap transition during this run. A configured trigger is not an observed switch. Without a trace or result, the timing and occurrence of any reduction should remain unstated.
How can the source acknowledge writes while Raft learners replay state?

Conceptually, learner preparation and source-quorum acknowledgment can proceed in parallel: the learners receive a snapshot and subsequent history, while pre-cutover writes are handled by the source’s authorized quorum. The run is meant to observe whether that overlap works in practice under WriteHot-1. It does not specify the exact quorum rules or report that the overlap succeeded.
Does the destination have to be at the latest log position at every moment for source acknowledgments to continue?

That is not the claim being evaluated. Learners may trail ongoing writes while preparing; the stated progress check is reaching a barrier index. The broader cutover must preserve writes acknowledged by the source, but temporary learner lag before ownership changes does not by itself determine acknowledgment continuity.

A barrier-catch-up observation alone should not be described as an ownership change.
Does the run exercise network partitions or a replica crash?

No partition or crash injection is specified for this 60-minute WriteHot-1 activity. It measures catch-up and acknowledgment continuity under the stated migration setup. It should not be presented as a safety finding across partitions or one replica crash.

Does the result say that writes stopped so the learners could catch up?

What precisely should I mean by acknowledgment continuity here?

The source quorum kept acknowledging writes during the learner migration. That is stronger than saying requests merely arrived at the source, but it is not a claim that every request was acknowledged immediately or that no request waited.
And is the 83% figure the fraction of write requests that received acknowledgments?
No. It is a throughput comparison: the reported migration throughput was 83% of migration-free throughput. It is not a success percentage for individual requests.
So if migration-free throughput is T, how should I express the reported rate?
As 0.83 × T for the reported comparison, where T represents migration-free throughput. That expresses the ratio without inventing an absolute operations-per-second value.
Does the figure tell us that throughput was exactly 83% at every moment until catch-up?

No time series or per-instant measurement is reported. The finding gives a throughput ratio of 83% alongside continued source-quorum acknowledgments and barrier catch-up in 42 minutes. It does not describe how throughput varied over that interval.
Can we infer how long the copy-on-write snapshot took from the catch-up time?

Can I conclude anything here about a network partition or one replica crash?

Does continuing to acknowledge writes prove that an acknowledged write would survive the eventual ownership change?

Would it be accurate to describe the learners as already authoritative once they reached the barrier?
