I’m injecting one replica crash and asymmetric network partitions during learner snapshot and replay. I want to verify that write acknowledgments remain quorum-gated and that the learners recover their progress toward the barrier after the partitions heal.

That tests two related but distinct behaviors while the destination is being prepared. Quorum-gated acknowledgments concern when a write may be reported as successful during a crash or partition. Learner barrier recovery concerns whether snapshot and replay progress can resume after communication heals. This describes the fault-injection activity and what it will verify; it does not report a result for either check.
Why inject faults during both the snapshot and replay portions?

The learners can be at different points in preparation during those portions. Interrupting snapshot work tests whether that interruption is handled without improperly changing acknowledgment authority; interrupting replay tests whether progress toward the barrier can recover. The activity does not specify exact injection instants or say that either portion has passed its check.
What makes a partition asymmetric in this context?

It means communication need not be disrupted identically for every participant. Some replicas or clients may be able to communicate along paths that others cannot use. That makes it important to check acknowledgment authority rather than assume everyone has the same view of learner progress or ownership. The particular network links affected are not specified here.
Is it enough to check whether the leader still receives write requests during a partition?

No. Receiving a request and acknowledging it are different. The named check is whether acknowledgments are quorum-gated: a leader that cannot satisfy the applicable quorum condition must not report a successful write merely because a client can reach it. The activity does not state the precise acknowledgment rule being exercised.
Does quorum-gated mean every write must wait for the destination learners?

Not necessarily. Learners preparing a destination and the quorum required to acknowledge a write are different concepts. The check is that each success follows the applicable quorum rule, not that learner receipt is automatically required for each write during snapshot or replay. Exactly which quorum applies at a given point depends on the ownership protocol, which this activity does not spell out.
What if one side of the asymmetric partition can acknowledge writes and the other cannot?

Different ability to make progress is not itself a safety violation. The important question is whether any acknowledgment issued by either side satisfies valid authority and quorum conditions, so that the partition cannot produce incompatible successful histories. The fault injection is intended to verify quorum-gated acknowledgments; no observation about which side can progress has been reported.
Would a request that waits for a quorum count as a failed check?

No. Waiting rather than acknowledging without the required quorum can be the safe behavior during a partition or crash. This activity checks the conditions for successful acknowledgments, not whether every request finishes despite the faults.
Why mention a single replica crash separately from the partitions?

They disrupt different things. A crash makes a replica unavailable; a partition changes who can communicate. Testing one replica crash alongside asymmetric partitions probes whether acknowledgment gating and learner preparation remain well-defined under that stated fault scope. It does not imply that two or more replica crashes are covered.
Does the activity tell us which replica crashes?

No. It specifies one replica crash during snapshot or replay, but does not identify that replica or give the crash schedule. We should not assume it is always a source replica, always a learner, or that a particular recovery mechanism is exercised.
Could a replica crash erase the barrier index the learners are aiming for?

Whether a crash affects the information needed to identify or reach the barrier depends on the protocol’s state and durability rules. The stated check is learner barrier recovery after the partitions heal, with one crash injected during snapshot or replay. The activity does not say how the barrier is stored or report whether any information was lost.
What should “barrier recovery after healing” mean without inventing a recovery algorithm?

It means checking whether learners can resume or establish the required catch-up to the barrier once the partitioned communication paths are restored. It should not be confused with merely hearing the barrier index: reaching the barrier concerns the required history through that point. The activity does not define a restart procedure, a completion time, or the observed recovery outcome.
Does healing the partition also undo the replica crash?

No. Network healing restores communication that the partition disrupted; it does not, by itself, restart a crashed replica. Interpreting the recovery check requires keeping those events distinct. The activity does not specify whether the crashed replica returns or which surviving replicas the learners use afterward.
If the learners eventually reach the barrier after healing, does that prove acknowledgments were safe during the partition?

No. Catching up afterward is a progress observation. Quorum-gated acknowledgments are a separate safety observation about successes issued while faults affected the system. The activity calls for checking both because later learner progress cannot retroactively justify an acknowledgment issued without valid authority.
Could acknowledgments be correctly gated while the learners never recover barrier progress?

Conceptually, yes. The store could refrain from unsafe acknowledgments yet leave migration unable to resume after healing. Conversely, learner progress would not excuse unsafe acknowledgments. The activity is designed to look at both properties, and it supplies no finding about either one.
Does reaching the barrier after healing mean the destination can immediately be promoted?

Not on its own. Barrier catch-up is a preparation condition, not the ownership transfer itself. The learner approach also calls for deduplication-state replication before joint reconfiguration. This fault-injection activity names barrier recovery and quorum-gated acknowledgments; it does not report that promotion occurred or that every reconfiguration prerequisite was satisfied.
Does this injection explicitly verify retry deduplication?

No retry-deduplication check is named. Retries remain relevant to safe migration, but the observations specified here are quorum-gated acknowledgments during the injected faults and learner barrier recovery after healing. A result on those checks should not be relabeled as a separate result for retries.
What if a write is acknowledged before the partition interrupts replay?

That acknowledged write still has to remain accounted for in a safe ownership transfer. The fault-injection activity specifically names acknowledgment gating and barrier recovery; it does not separately report a write-survival check or an ownership cutover. We should not infer from a learner eventually reaching the barrier that every acknowledged-write-survival case has already been verified.
Could I use acknowledgment continuity as the success criterion here?

Not by itself. During faults, the source may be unable to obtain the required quorum, in which case withholding acknowledgment can protect safety. The criterion named for this activity is **quorum-gated** acknowledgments, not uninterrupted acknowledgments regardless of partition or crash.
Will this activity determine whether migration maintains at least 80% of migration-free throughput?

No throughput measurement is stated. The 80% target applies without failures during migration under continuous writes. This activity injects a replica crash and asymmetric partitions during snapshot and replay, then checks acknowledgment gating and barrier recovery. It should not be presented as a no-failure throughput benchmark.
What should I report if a learner stalls until the partition heals?

Report the observed stall and whether it subsequently reaches the barrier, if those are the observations. Stalling while communication is disrupted is different from failing to recover after healing. The activity does not yet state that either event occurred or set a deadline for recovery.
What is the narrowest useful description of what I’m verifying?

With one replica crash and asymmetric partitions injected during snapshot or replay, check that successful writes remain subject to the applicable quorum and that learners can recover barrier-index catch-up after the network heals. That is a specific failure at the promotion boundary. Restoring the key data and reaching the barrier did not ensure the dedup checkpoint accompanied them in those two trials. Does restoring the key data mean the transfer preserved everything it needed?

Could I describe this simply as lost key-value data?

That would misstate the observation. The key data was restored. What was omitted was the dedup checkpoint, and the reported effect was duplicate application of an acknowledged retry. The finding does not report a missing key or a lost value.
Why is the checkpoint relevant if the keys have been restored?

Key data describes the shard’s state, while the dedup checkpoint carries information relevant to recognizing a request across retries. Those are different parts of the handoff. The two reported trials show that restoring one did not ensure the other was present at promotion.
Does this mean barrier-index catch-up was never reached?

No. The finding describes *barrier-index promotion* that restored key data but omitted the dedup checkpoint. It does not say catch-up failed. The important distinction is that reaching a key-data or log barrier is not, by itself, evidence that the dedup checkpoint was included.
Can I infer that the checkpoint had never been generated or replicated anywhere?
No. The reported fact is that promotion omitted it. The finding does not identify where a checkpoint existed beforehand, how it was transferred, or why it was absent from the promoted state.
What does “applied twice” establish about the retry?

It establishes a duplicated application in the two reported trials, despite the retry being acknowledged. That is the concrete outcome. The finding does not specify the write operation, its value, the client’s complete response history, or how the duplicate application appeared in later reads.
Should I say every retry after barrier-index promotion was applied twice?

No. The observation is limited to two of 10,000 partition/crash trials. It identifies a possible duplicate-application outcome in those trials, not a general outcome for every retry or every promotion.
Do we know which replica crashed or what the asymmetric partition looked like in those two trials?

No. They occurred among partition/crash trials, but this finding does not identify the crashed replica, the affected communication paths, or the precise fault timing. Those details should not be supplied as an explanation without a trace.
Could the duplicate be dismissed if applying the same write happens to be harmless?

The finding does not say the operation was harmless or that applying it twice was intended. Its stated concern is that an acknowledged retry was applied twice when the dedup checkpoint was omitted. Does the observation tell us that acknowledgments stopped being quorum-gated?

No. It reports a missing dedup checkpoint and duplicate application during barrier-index promotion. It does not give a separate finding about whether the acknowledgment satisfied the applicable quorum rule. Quorum gating and retry deduplication are distinct checks.
What about learner recovery after the partition heals—did it fail in those trials?

No learner-recovery outcome is stated here. The finding says promotion restored key data, omitted the dedup checkpoint, and applied an acknowledged retry twice in two trials. It does not say whether, when, or how learners recovered after healing.
Is it fair to say that promotion needs to account for deduplication state as well as key data?

Yes, as the direct issue exposed by the observation. In the two trials, restoring key data without the dedup checkpoint did not preserve the intended handling of an acknowledged retry. The result identifies what was missing at promotion; it does not specify a completed fix or a verified new promotion rule.
Can I claim from this result that all operations were non-linearizable?

That would be much broader than the reported outcome. The concrete finding is that an acknowledged retry was applied twice in two partition/crash trials. It raises a correctness concern for retry handling across promotion, but it does not provide a classification of every operation history in those trials.
Does two in 10,000 tell us how often the issue will happen in production?

No. It is the observed frequency among these 10,000 injected partition/crash trials. The trial count demonstrates that the behavior occurred in the tested setup, but it does not establish a production probability or a frequency under different schedules.
Could the throughput and catch-up measurements answer whether this retry problem is resolved?

No. Throughput and catch-up concern performance and transfer progress. They cannot show that a dedup checkpoint accompanies key data at promotion or that an acknowledged retry avoids duplicate application. This finding is a separate correctness observation.
What is the most precise short report of the result?

In 2/10,000 partition/crash trials, barrier-index promotion restored key data but omitted the dedup checkpoint, and an acknowledged retry was applied twice. That states the frequency, the missing state, and the observed consequence without assuming an unstated cause or remedy.
How can promotion guarantee learners durably install deduplication state through the barrier index before serving retried writes?

Promotion needs a readiness condition that covers two things, not just one: the learners must have the required shard history through the barrier index, and they must have durably installed the corresponding deduplication state. Serving retried writes must remain gated until that condition is established. The question does not specify the exact protocol for recording readiness or changing authority, so this is the guarantee the protocol needs to enforce, not a claim that it already does.
Why isn’t reaching the barrier index enough?

Reaching the barrier establishes a point in the shard’s ordered history. It does not, by itself, establish that a learner has the request-identification information needed to recognize an earlier attempt when a client retries. A destination could have the key data through the barrier yet handle a retry without knowing its prior outcome. Promotion has to account for both kinds of state.
What does “through the barrier index” add to the deduplication requirement?

It ties the deduplication state to a definite point in the history the learners are expected to have installed. Otherwise, saying merely that some deduplication state was transferred would leave open whether it covers requests associated with the history through that barrier. The exact relationship between a request’s outcome, its deduplication record, and the index needs to be specified by the protocol.
Could a learner report that it received the deduplication checkpoint and then be promoted?

Receipt alone is weaker than durable installation. The question asks for a guarantee that the state is installed before retried writes are served, including when a replica crashes within the stated fault scope. A promotion rule would need evidence of the required durable state, rather than relying only on a message saying a checkpoint arrived.
What distinction are you making between replication and installation?

Replicating deduplication state describes getting it to the destination; installing it describes making it part of the state the learner will actually use to handle requests. A transferred record that is not yet installed could leave a promoted replica unable to recognize a retry. “Durably” further requires that the relevant installed information not disappear merely because transient state is lost. The question does not prescribe how those stages are represented.
Does the state have to be durable before promotion, or is it enough to make it durable before the first retry arrives?

The question places durable installation before serving retried writes. One way to make that boundary unambiguous is to make it a prerequisite for promotion to serving authority. If promotion can happen earlier, the protocol would still need an effective gate that prevents retried writes from being served until installation is durable. Simply expecting the checkpoint to finish before a retry happens would not be a guarantee.
What if the promotion decision is made while one learner is still installing the deduplication state?

The design would need to define whether that learner can serve requests at that point. It must not serve a retried write as an owner while lacking the required durable deduplication state through the barrier. The question does not settle whether promotion waits for every learner or which replicas may serve, so a precise protocol would need to connect readiness to serving authority.
Are you saying every learner must install the checkpoint, even if only some will serve?

The question refers to learners installing the state, but it does not specify a readiness count or a serving subset. The essential guarantee is that a replica cannot serve a retried write on newly acquired authority while missing the required deduplication information. A full design must say which learners need durable installation for promotion and how that condition remains safe through one replica crash; I would not assume a particular count from the question alone.
Could the new owner fetch missing deduplication information on demand when a retry appears?

That could only answer the question if serving the retry waited until the needed information had been obtained and its outcome could be determined safely. Treating a missing record as proof that the request is new would not guarantee correct handling. On-demand fetching would be an additional mechanism to specify, not something established by the proposed learner handoff.
Why can’t an absent request ID in the destination state just mean the client’s first attempt failed?

The client may retry because it did not receive a response, and the earlier attempt’s outcome can be uncertain from the client’s perspective. If deduplication state is incomplete, absence of an ID at the destination says little about that outcome. The destination must not convert a gap in transferred information into a conclusion that the request never took effect.
Does the barrier itself need to cover the deduplication record, or can the checkpoint be tracked separately?

Either representation would need a precise consistency rule. What matters is that, before a replica serves retried writes, its durable deduplication state covers the relevant request outcomes through the barrier index and is consistent with the shard history it installed. A barrier for key data and an unrelated checkpoint-completion flag would not establish that relationship without an additional rule. The question does not choose a representation.
What if the learner has durable key data but only an in-memory deduplication table?

That would not meet the durable-installation condition for deduplication state. A crash could leave the learner retaining the key data but no longer knowing that a retried request corresponds to an earlier outcome. The guarantee requires the information needed for retry handling to remain available within the stated one-replica-crash scope.
Can the source keep serving writes while learners install that state?

The question does not require stopping source writes during learner preparation. What it requires is a coherent boundary: as source operations continue, the destination’s barrier history and deduplication state must be made consistent with the outcomes it may encounter when it starts serving retries. A complete protocol would have to specify how it handles operations at and beyond that boundary; durable installation through the barrier alone does not answer every later-write case.
What does ‘serving a retried write’ mean for the order of operations?

It means the destination handles a new attempt that may refer to an operation already handled elsewhere. Its response and any effect must fit the same linearizable history as the earlier attempt. Before doing that, it needs both authority to serve and reliable information about the earlier request’s outcome. Having authority without the necessary deduplication state would leave those questions disconnected.
If the earlier write was acknowledged, should the destination apply it again to answer the retry?

It must handle the retry consistently with the already acknowledged outcome, without introducing a second incompatible effect. That requires the relevant deduplication information to be available when the retry is served. The question does not specify the exact response or the form in which the outcome is recorded.
Could a checkpoint be durable yet still be the wrong checkpoint for the barrier?

Yes, as a general distinction. Durability says the installed checkpoint survives as required; coverage says it contains the information needed through the barrier index. A durable checkpoint that covers an earlier point would not establish the requested guarantee. The promotion condition needs to check both its durability and its relationship to the barrier.
What happens if a partition prevents a learner from receiving the deduplication state but it has the shard snapshot?

The snapshot alone cannot establish readiness to serve retried writes. If the learner cannot acquire and durably install the required deduplication state, the protocol must not treat its possession of key data as sufficient serving authority for retries. The broader goal does not promise that every request remains available during a partition; it does require safe outcomes.
Does healing the partition automatically make that learner ready?

No. Restored communication creates an opportunity to transfer and install missing state. Readiness would still require verifying that the learner has durably installed the deduplication state covering the barrier, along with the necessary shard history. Healing a network path is not the same as completing those steps.
What if a learner reports readiness and then crashes before serving any requests?

The word ‘durably’ is intended to make readiness meaningful across that kind of interruption. The protocol would need to ensure that any replica allowed to serve after the crash still has, or can safely establish, the required installed history and deduplication state. A readiness report based solely on volatile information would not provide that assurance. The question does not specify a recovery procedure.
Could we check only that a deduplication checkpoint exists somewhere in the destination configuration?

Existence somewhere is not automatically enough for a replica that is about to serve a retry. The guarantee must connect the required checkpoint to the authority and state of whichever learners are permitted to answer. Exactly how many durable copies are required depends on the configuration and serving rules, which are not given here.
How would I state the promotion condition without choosing a storage engine or message protocol?

State it as an invariant on authority: no learner may serve a retried write after promotion unless the required shard history and deduplication state through the barrier index have been durably installed and are consistent with the prior request outcomes. The specific mechanism for establishing and checking that condition can then be defined separately.
Is that an assertion that the Raft learner proposal already guarantees it?

No. It is the property the promotion rule needs to guarantee. Staging destination replicas as Raft learners, catching up to a barrier index, and replicating deduplication state identify the relevant pieces, but they do not alone tell us when installation is durable or when a learner gains permission to serve a retried write.
What is the cleanest question to ask when reviewing a proposed promotion rule?

Ask whether any learner can begin serving a retried write after promotion while its durable deduplication state is missing an outcome covered by the barrier-index history it claims to have installed. If that execution is possible, the rule has not established the requested guarantee; if it is excluded, the reason must hold across the relevant crash and partition conditions.

Given the 42-minute learner catch-up at 83% of migration-free throughput, my hypothesis is that atomic key-and-dedup barrier persistence should prevent duplicate retries while retaining at least 80% of migration-free throughput.

That connects a correctness hypothesis to a performance constraint. At the barrier, the key data and deduplication state would need to become durably available together, so promotion cannot expose the keys while leaving out information needed to recognize a retry. The 42-minute catch-up and 83% throughput provide context, but they do not show that adding atomic persistence prevents duplicate retries or keeps throughput at or above 80%. Both parts remain predictions.
What exactly needs to be atomic? Is it enough that both pieces are eventually persisted?

The relevant atomicity is at the barrier used to determine readiness for serving: promotion must not be able to observe the required key history as durably installed while the matching deduplication state is absent. Eventual persistence would leave a possible gap in which retried writes are served with incomplete information. The hypothesis does not prescribe a particular way to create that all-or-nothing condition.
Does atomic key-and-dedup persistence mean every key update and request ID must be written in one physical operation?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis states a property of the durable barrier and what promotion may rely on, not a physical write format. Whatever mechanism implements it must make the key and deduplication information needed through that barrier inseparable for the purpose of readiness. No storage-engine technique is specified.
Why tie deduplication state to the barrier rather than simply checking that some checkpoint exists?

Fsync latency could be useful additional information, but it would not by itself answer the stated throughput question. The relevant measure is operation throughput during migration with the adopted checkpoint gate, relative to migration-free throughput under the required continuous-write, no-failure condition.
Should I say this decision completes the validation of learner migration?

No. It adopts the checkpoint safeguard and provisionally retains learner streaming, then explicitly calls for another throughput benchmark. It does not report throughput with the gate or establish that every migration and retry behavior has been validated.
What should a short decision statement retain to avoid implying that the 83% was measured after the gate?

“Provisionally retain learner streaming based on its **pre-gate 83% throughput** result; adopt **quorum-fsynced atomic checkpoints** against duplicate retries, then **rebenchmark throughput** with the gate included.” That preserves the decision, the timing of the measurement, and the open performance question.
I propose offloading snapshots to object storage for the Raft learners, then jointly reconfiguring ownership only after key-and-dedup barriers have been fsynced by a destination quorum.

That separates destination preparation from the authority change. Object storage would carry snapshots for the learners, while the quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barriers would be a prerequisite for joint reconfiguration. This is a proposal, not a finding that the resulting migration preserves every acknowledged write or meets the throughput target.
What does offloading snapshots to object storage mean for the learners?

It means using object storage as the place from which the Raft learners obtain snapshot data during preparation. It does not, by itself, make those learners caught up, give them ownership, or establish that the snapshot contains writes made after its view of the shard was taken. The proposal does not specify how snapshots are written to or retrieved from object storage.
Is object storage supposed to replace Raft replication?

The proposal says to offload snapshots for Raft learners, not to replace Raft or its ownership rules. Snapshot delivery and agreement on who may serve operations are different concerns. Joint reconfiguration remains the proposed ownership-transfer step, subject to the stated barrier prerequisite.
Could the destination be promoted as soon as it downloads a snapshot?

No. The proposal explicitly permits joint reconfiguration only after the key-and-dedup barriers have been fsynced by a destination quorum. Obtaining a snapshot from object storage does not establish that prerequisite, even if it gives a learner a useful starting view of the shard.
Why do we need a barrier if the snapshot contains the keys?

Key data alone does not account for all the information needed at the ownership boundary. The barrier pairs key history with deduplication state, which matters when a client retries an operation across the handoff. Also, a snapshot is a view of state; writes may continue while learners prepare. The proposal does not spell out the full catch-up procedure, so the snapshot should not be mistaken for a complete promotion condition.
What does the ‘key-and-dedup’ part require conceptually?

The state used to serve keys and the state used to recognize previously handled request IDs must correspond at the barrier. If the destination became authoritative with key data but without matching deduplication information, it could handle a retry without knowing the earlier outcome. The proposal names the paired barrier but does not define its storage format or coverage rule.
Does the object-store snapshot have to carry the deduplication state too?

That is not specified. The proposal states that snapshots are offloaded to object storage and that joint reconfiguration waits for quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barriers. It does not say where deduplication state resides inside the snapshot, whether it is transferred separately, or how the two transfers are coordinated.
What exactly must be fsynced before reconfiguration?

The stated prerequisite is the key-and-dedup barriers, fsynced by a destination quorum. It would be inaccurate to substitute ‘a snapshot was uploaded’ or ‘one learner received the data’ for that condition. The proposal does not define the precise bytes in a barrier or the evidence used to confirm the quorum fsync.
Does a single destination replica reporting an fsync meet the rule?

No. The requirement is a destination **quorum** fsync, not a single replica’s report. Equally, the proposal does not say that every destination replica must fsync before joint reconfiguration. The quorum condition is the scope expressly stated.
Why put the fsync condition before joint reconfiguration instead of finishing it immediately afterward?

Joint reconfiguration changes ownership authority. If it could proceed before the destination quorum durably held the matching key-and-dedup barriers, newly authorized service might depend on information that had not satisfied the proposed durability gate. ‘Only after’ makes that gate a prerequisite, not a cleanup step.
Would an object-storage upload count as the quorum fsync?

Not under the wording of the proposal. Offloading a snapshot to object storage and fsyncing a key-and-dedup barrier at a destination quorum are distinct operations. The proposal gives no rule equating object-store persistence with a destination replica’s fsync, much less with fsyncs by a destination quorum.
Suppose the learners have snapshot data but the barrier cannot reach a destination quorum because of a partition. Can reconfiguration go ahead?

Not under the proposed ordering. The destination-quorum fsync prerequisite would still be unmet. Holding back joint reconfiguration may limit progress during a partition, but the goal requires safe ownership transfer, not successful promotion regardless of communication failures.
And if a replica crashes after the barrier is fsynced, is crash safety automatically established?

The quorum-fsync prerequisite is intended to make promotion rely on durable destination state rather than on a single temporary copy. But the proposal alone does not establish every recovery rule or prove preservation of acknowledged writes through one replica crash. That conclusion would require showing that the barrier contents and ownership rules continue to provide the necessary history after the crash.
Does a learner holding a snapshot have authority to answer a retried write?

Snapshot possession alone grants no stated serving authority. The proposal places ownership transfer at joint reconfiguration and requires the quorum-fsynced barriers before that step. A retry needs to be handled consistently with its earlier outcome by whichever configuration is authorized to serve; merely having key data is insufficient to infer that outcome.
Could object storage make snapshot streaming free for foreground writes?

No such performance effect is established. Offloading changes where snapshots are supplied from, but preparing, transferring, and installing them may still consume resources. The separate no-failure performance target is at least 80% of migration-free throughput while migrating a shard under continuous writes. This proposal provides no throughput measurement for object-store snapshot offload.
Do we know whether object storage will make migration faster or slower?

No. The proposal specifies the offload approach, not snapshot-transfer time, learner catch-up time, or cutover latency. Its effect on migration progress and operation throughput remains to be assessed; neither a speedup nor a slowdown can be inferred from the storage location alone.
Is the snapshot enough to protect a write acknowledged while it is being transferred?

Not by itself. A snapshot may reflect an earlier view, while writes continue and are acknowledged. The ownership-transfer rules must ensure that acknowledged writes remain in the history the destination retains. The proposed key-and-dedup barriers and joint reconfiguration are relevant to that obligation, but their exact treatment of writes during snapshot transfer is not specified here.
Does the barrier condition also matter for retries whose earlier response was lost?

Yes, conceptually. A client may retry without knowing whether its earlier attempt took effect. Matching durable deduplication information to the key history at the barrier is intended to prevent the destination from treating missing knowledge as proof that the request is new. The proposal does not define the request-ID records or prove that every such retry is covered.
Can I call this a complete protocol for network partitions and one replica crash?

Not yet. It identifies snapshot offload, Raft learners, a destination-quorum durability prerequisite for key-and-dedup barriers, and joint reconfiguration. To establish the full goal, the authority rules, barrier coverage, and behavior under retries, partitions, and one replica crash still need to be precise and validated. The proposal does not provide those results.
What would be misleading about saying object storage is the new shard owner?

Object storage is proposed as a snapshot source for the learners, not as a configuration that serves linearizable key-value operations. Ownership is transferred through joint reconfiguration after the destination-quorum-fsynced barriers. Conflating snapshot location with serving authority would obscure that distinction.
How would you state the proposed ordering without adding a transfer protocol?

Offload snapshots to object storage for Raft learners; require a destination quorum to fsync the key-and-dedup barriers; only then jointly reconfigure ownership. That preserves the explicit promotion prerequisite without assuming how snapshots, further history, or barrier acknowledgments are transported.
Does the proposal choose a transfer cap or a throughput trigger?

No. It does not specify an egress percentage, trigger threshold, or scheduling policy. Object-store offload may be evaluated against the at-least-80% migration-free-throughput requirement under continuous writes, but the proposal contains neither a chosen numerical throttle nor a measured performance result.
What is the main correctness distinction I should keep visible when discussing it?

Preparing learners with object-store snapshots is not the same as authorizing them to serve. Joint reconfiguration must wait until a destination quorum has fsynced matching key-and-dedup barriers, so key history and retry information are not treated as independently ready at promotion. Whether that rule fully preserves linearizability and acknowledged writes across the required failures is still an open validation question.
Can object-storage snapshots reduce source egress while preserving learner catch-up and quorum-fsynced barrier consistency?

Potentially, but those are three separate things to establish. Serving a snapshot to Raft learners from object storage could reduce the source’s direct snapshot traffic. The learners would still need to catch up with writes beyond the snapshot, and joint reconfiguration must still wait for a destination quorum to fsync the matching key-and-dedup barriers. The question does not provide an egress measurement or show that either readiness condition is met.
Why wouldn’t putting the snapshot in object storage automatically reduce source egress?

The snapshot has to reach object storage somehow, and other migration traffic may still leave the source. Offloading could change who serves snapshot downloads without eliminating all source egress. To establish a reduction, we would need to measure source egress for the relevant migration traffic, rather than infer it solely from where learners retrieve the snapshot.
Should I distinguish snapshot traffic from the traffic used to catch learners up?

Yes. Snapshot delivery supplies a starting view; learner catch-up accounts for the history needed beyond that view. A lower source cost for distributing snapshots would not automatically mean the remaining catch-up traffic is smaller or that learners reach the required barrier index. The question asks for both an egress benefit and preserved catch-up.
Could learners finish downloading the object-storage snapshot and be considered caught up?

Not on that basis alone. Writes can continue after the snapshot’s view of the shard. Learners have to reach the barrier index specified for the ownership transfer. Completing the download establishes that they have the snapshot, not that their history has advanced through the barrier.
If writes remain continuous, is the barrier a moving target?

A specified barrier index is a defined point in the history, even though newer writes may continue to arrive. Learner catch-up to that point is meaningful without assuming that the latest log position stops moving. The ownership rules still have to account for operations around and beyond that point; the question does not define those rules.
What would preserving learner catch-up mean when comparing object storage with another snapshot source?

At minimum, learners would still need to acquire the snapshot and reach the required barrier index under the intended ongoing-write condition. Merely shifting download traffic away from the source would not establish that they can make that progress. The question supplies no catch-up time or completion observation for object-storage snapshots.
Could object storage itself certify that the barrier is ready?

Storing a snapshot is different from establishing destination readiness. The proposed cutover condition requires key-and-dedup barriers fsynced by a destination quorum before joint reconfiguration. An object-store upload or download cannot simply be substituted for those destination-quorum fsyncs.
Why does the barrier have to include deduplication state as well as keys?

Key state alone may not tell a newly serving replica whether a retried request has already taken effect. A matching key-and-dedup barrier ties the relevant shard history to the information needed for consistent retry handling. Offloading the snapshot must not let promotion proceed with the keys ready but the corresponding deduplication state missing.
Does the snapshot necessarily contain that matching deduplication state?

The question does not say. Regardless of where that state is transferred from, barrier consistency requires the destination to establish a matching, durable key-and-dedup view through the barrier before reconfiguration. We should not assume that placing the snapshot in object storage automatically carries or installs the needed deduplication information.
What if a learner has the keys through the barrier but its deduplication checkpoint is still being installed?

That learner’s key progress would not, by itself, establish the paired barrier condition. The requirement is for the matching key-and-dedup barrier to be fsynced by a destination quorum before joint reconfiguration. A pending deduplication installation cannot be treated as completed merely because the key data has arrived.
Does a destination quorum just need to receive the checkpoint?

No. The condition is quorum **fsync** of the key-and-dedup barrier, not mere receipt. The destination quorum’s durable readiness must be established before jointly changing ownership. Exactly how that condition is represented and checked is not supplied by this question.
Would a partition make object-storage access enough to promote even if the destination quorum cannot fsync?

No. A learner’s ability to retrieve a snapshot does not waive the destination-quorum durability condition. If the required quorum cannot fsync the matching barrier, joint reconfiguration cannot rely on that barrier as complete. The safety requirement does not promise promotion during a partition.
Could offloading snapshots make acknowledgments on the source faster?

It might reduce competition from direct snapshot distribution, but the question reports no acknowledgment or throughput measurement. Other work, including making the snapshot available and advancing learner history, may still consume resources. Source-egress reduction and faster foreground acknowledgments are different claims that would each need evidence.
If I see a source-egress reduction, can I conclude the overall throughput target is met?

No. The no-failure target is at least 80% of migration-free operation throughput while a shard migrates under continuous writes. Source egress is a resource-use measurement, not the operation-throughput ratio. Reducing it would not, by itself, establish that numerical target or that the learners catch up.
What if learner catch-up succeeds but the destination-quorum barrier has not been fsynced?

That would show progress toward the barrier index, but not satisfy the stated pre-reconfiguration durability condition. The destination must not be treated as ready to jointly reconfigure solely because its learners caught up in key history. The key-and-dedup barrier still needs its destination-quorum fsync.
Conversely, could a quorum-fsynced barrier tell me how much source egress was saved?

No. It is a consistency and durability condition for ownership transfer. It does not quantify source traffic. The egress question requires a separate measurement covering snapshot offload and whatever source traffic remains during learner catch-up.
Is reduced source egress guaranteed to make catch-up faster?

No. Offload changes where snapshot traffic is served from; it does not specify snapshot availability, learner download speed, or replay progress. Catch-up could not be inferred from the direction of an egress change. The question asks whether both properties can hold, not whether one automatically causes the other.
What comparisons would directly answer the source-egress part without treating it as a safety result?

Compare source egress during otherwise comparable shard migrations with and without object-storage snapshot offload, while identifying which traffic is counted. Then separately observe whether learners reach the barrier index and whether the matching key-and-dedup barriers receive the required destination-quorum fsync before joint reconfiguration. The question provides no measured values for any of those observations.
Do those checks also establish linearizability across retries, partitions, and a replica crash?

Not automatically. Catch-up and quorum-fsynced barrier consistency are necessary concerns for the proposed transfer, especially for retry information, but full linearizability and acknowledged-write survival also depend on the ownership and acknowledgment rules. An egress measurement says still less about failure-case safety. No result covering all of those behaviors is stated in this question.
What is the shortest faithful answer to the original question?

Object-storage snapshots may reduce direct source snapshot egress, but that benefit must be measured. Learners must still catch up to the barrier index, and joint reconfiguration must remain gated on a destination quorum fsyncing matching key-and-dedup barriers. Snapshot offload alone establishes neither catch-up nor barrier consistency.
My hypothesis is that object-storage snapshots halve source egress compared with direct streaming, while Raft learners still catch up within 60 minutes and barrier durability remains intact.

That makes three predictions, all of which need to hold together: source egress with object-storage snapshots is about half the direct-streaming baseline, learners reach catch-up within 60 minutes, and the barrier remains durably established. It is a hypothesis, not a measured reduction, catch-up result, or durability finding.
What is the comparison behind “halve source egress”?

Direct streaming is the comparison baseline. If its measured source egress were E under comparable conditions, halving it would mean measuring about E/2 with object-storage snapshots. The hypothesis supplies no value for E and does not claim that source egress falls to zero.
Should the comparison count only the source traffic used to deliver the snapshot?

That depends on how source egress is defined for the comparison. If the claim is about total source egress during migration, excluding traffic used to make the snapshot available or to support learner catch-up could overstate the reduction. The hypothesis does not define an accounting boundary, so a test should state it explicitly and use it consistently for object-storage snapshots and direct streaming.
Does using object storage mean the source no longer sends any migration data?

Not necessarily. Learners still need to catch up beyond the snapshot’s view, and placing a snapshot in object storage may itself involve source traffic. The prediction is a halving of source egress versus direct streaming, not elimination of all traffic from the source.
Could learner downloads from object storage be counted as source egress?

Traffic sent by object storage to learners is distinct from traffic sent by the source replicas. That distinction is the point of measuring *source* egress. It does not mean the object-storage downloads have no network cost; the hypothesis makes a claim about source egress, not total traffic across every component.
Could I show a 50% reduction by comparing migrations with different write workloads?

That would make the comparison difficult to interpret. Continuing writes can affect traffic and learner catch-up, so the direct-streaming baseline and object-storage case need comparable conditions if the measured difference is to bear on the snapshot-offload hypothesis. No particular write rate or workload is specified here.
Why is learner catch-up a separate condition instead of a consequence of the egress reduction?

Moving snapshot delivery away from the source might reduce its outbound traffic without ensuring that learners receive and replay everything needed to reach the barrier. Egress and catch-up describe different outcomes. The hypothesis requires both lower source egress and learner catch-up within 60 minutes.
Does “within 60 minutes” refer to downloading the snapshot?

It refers to the learners catching up, not merely completing a snapshot download. Snapshot receipt can be an initial step, but writes may continue afterward. A download that finishes inside 60 minutes does not, by itself, establish that the learners reached the required barrier within that period.
If a learner knows the barrier index but is still replaying writes, has it caught up?

No. Learning which index to reach is different from having the needed history through it. The 60-minute prediction is about catch-up, so its completion condition needs to reflect the learner actually reaching the barrier rather than just receiving its identifier.
Do continuous writes make the 60-minute condition impossible to interpret?

No. A barrier provides a defined point in the history even if later writes keep arriving. A measurement can ask when the learners reach that point. The hypothesis does not specify how the barrier is chosen or how operations beyond it are handled at ownership change.
Suppose the snapshot comes from object storage and the learners catch up in 59 minutes, but source egress barely changes. Would the hypothesis hold?

No. Catching up within 60 minutes would satisfy one prediction, but the predicted halving of source egress would not be established. The three outcomes should be reported separately rather than treating timely catch-up as evidence for an egress reduction.
And if source egress is halved but catch-up takes more than 60 minutes?

That would support the egress part under a valid comparison, but miss the stated catch-up bound. The hypothesis does not permit trading an arbitrarily slow catch-up for a 50% source-egress reduction and then calling the whole prediction satisfied.
What exactly does ‘barrier durability remains intact’ mean here?

It means the snapshot offload must not weaken the durable barrier prerequisite for ownership transfer. In the proposed approach, joint reconfiguration waits for key-and-dedup barriers fsynced by a destination quorum. Retrieving a snapshot from object storage cannot substitute for that destination-quorum durability condition.
Would a successfully stored object be enough evidence of barrier durability?

No. Object storage holding a snapshot and a destination quorum fsyncing the matching key-and-dedup barriers are different conditions. The hypothesis predicts an egress benefit while retaining the barrier’s durability rule; it does not propose replacing that rule with proof that a snapshot object exists.
If the destination quorum has the keys but not matching deduplication state, is durability intact?

Not for the key-and-dedup barrier at issue. The durable condition must cover matching key and deduplication state through the barrier. Durable key data alone would not establish that a newly serving replica can recognize relevant retried requests.
Does the barrier have to be durable before the learners start downloading the snapshot?

The stated prerequisite is before joint reconfiguration, not necessarily before snapshot retrieval begins. The hypothesis does not specify an order between beginning the object-storage download and establishing the durable barrier. What must not happen is treating snapshot delivery or catch-up as permission to bypass the barrier condition when ownership changes.
Could I call the barriers intact just because no write loss is observed in one ordinary run?

That observation alone would be narrower. Barrier durability concerns whether the matching state satisfies the destination-quorum durability requirement, including when durability matters under the intended fault conditions. Not seeing a lost write in one run would not itself show that the quorum fsync occurred or that the barrier was correctly paired with deduplication state.
Are we predicting that object storage makes the quorum fsync faster?

No. The hypothesis predicts half the source egress versus direct streaming, catch-up within 60 minutes, and intact barrier durability. It gives no predicted fsync latency, cutover latency, or speedup in establishing the barrier.
Is the 60-minute catch-up bound also a guarantee that promotion completes within 60 minutes?

No. Catch-up and promotion are separate milestones. Joint reconfiguration still depends on the quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barrier. The hypothesis provides a proposed catch-up bound, not a bound on the complete ownership transfer.
Does halving source egress establish the at-least-80% operation-throughput target?

No. Source egress is a resource-use measure, whereas the performance goal compares operation throughput during continuous-write migration against migration-free throughput. An egress reduction could be relevant to that goal, but this hypothesis does not predict a throughput ratio or provide a throughput measurement.
Can we say the object-storage version is safer than direct streaming?

The hypothesis does not make that comparison. It predicts an egress reduction while barrier durability stays intact; it does not claim improved safety relative to direct streaming. The ownership and acknowledgment rules would still need to preserve linearizability and acknowledged writes.
What if object storage is unavailable during part of the transfer?

That could prevent learners from making the expected progress, but no object-storage failure scenario or availability guarantee is specified in the hypothesis. The appropriate response is not to assume that catch-up still finishes within 60 minutes, or to waive the durable barrier prerequisite. Such a failure would need its own stated scope and evidence.
What could an evaluation report without merging all three predictions into one number?

It could report source egress for object-storage snapshots alongside the comparable direct-streaming value, whether and when learners reached the barrier relative to the 60-minute bound, and whether the matching key-and-dedup barriers met the destination-quorum fsync condition before reconfiguration. Those observations address the three predictions individually. None is supplied yet.
Could a measurement show the source sent less snapshot data without proving source egress was halved overall?

Yes. A reduction in direct snapshot-serving traffic may be offset by other source outbound traffic, depending on what the measurement includes. The wording ‘halve source egress versus direct streaming’ calls for a like-for-like source-egress comparison, not only a count of bytes sent on one snapshot path.
What if the measured ratio is 51% of the direct-streaming baseline?

That would be close to half, but not an exact halving. Whether ‘halve’ permits an approximate result should be made clear when evaluating the hypothesis rather than silently turning a measured ratio into exactly 50%. No such measurement is reported here; 51% is only an illustration.
How should I phrase this as a hypothesis without implying a completed benchmark or safety check?

Hypothesis: object-storage snapshots for Raft learners reduce source egress to about half that of direct streaming, while learners reach barrier catch-up within 60 minutes and the destination-quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barrier condition remains intact. Source egress, catch-up, and barrier durability each remain to be evaluated.
I plan to upload a versioned, checksummed copy-on-write snapshot for the Raft learners. I’ll compare source egress and learner catch-up against direct streaming, then fault-inject barrier promotion.

That plan examines snapshot offload on two fronts before probing the ownership boundary. The versioned, checksummed snapshot provides an identifiable snapshot artifact whose integrity can be checked. Comparing with direct streaming addresses both source egress and learner catch-up; fault-injecting barrier promotion addresses whether the promotion condition remains safe when faults occur. These are planned activities, not results.
Why make the snapshot versioned?

A version lets the transfer refer to a particular snapshot rather than an unspecified or changing copy. That matters when relating the learners’ starting state to subsequent catch-up and the barrier. The plan does not specify a version format, how versions are chosen, or how a version is tied to a log position.
What does the checksum contribute?

It provides a way to check that the snapshot being used matches the uploaded snapshot artifact. That is an integrity check on transferred snapshot content, not proof that the snapshot contains all later writes, that learners have caught up, or that the key-and-dedup barrier has been durably established. No checksum algorithm or validation result is stated.
Does a checksummed snapshot mean we no longer need barrier catch-up?

No. A checksum can help verify the snapshot’s contents, but a snapshot represents a view of the shard at a point in its history. Continuous writes can extend that history while learners obtain the snapshot. Learner catch-up remains a separate outcome to compare against direct streaming.
When you say upload, is the destination receiving its snapshot directly from the source?

The plan is for an object-storage snapshot: upload the copy-on-write snapshot so it can serve as the learners’ snapshot source. That differs from directly streaming the snapshot to the learners. Should the upload itself count when I compare source egress?

The comparison should state its accounting boundary. If the upload sends data from the source, ignoring that traffic while counting direct-streaming traffic would make a total source-egress comparison misleading. The plan says to compare source egress against direct streaming, but it does not define precisely which traffic the measurement includes.
Could I claim the offload saves source egress just because learners download from object storage?

Not yet. Learner downloads being served elsewhere could reduce direct source-to-learner snapshot traffic, but the source may still send the upload and other migration traffic. The planned source-egress comparison, rather than the choice of snapshot location alone, is what can establish whether egress is reduced.
What is the proper baseline for that comparison?

Direct streaming is the named baseline. Measure source egress for the object-storage snapshot approach and for direct streaming under comparable conditions, then compare the two. The plan supplies neither measurement nor a resulting reduction.
Could I compare source egress from one run with catch-up time from a different run and call that a result?

That would make the tradeoff difficult to interpret. Each approach should be described with its own source-egress and catch-up observations under comparable conditions. The plan does not specify a benchmark procedure or the number of runs, so it is better to keep the two measurements distinct without inventing a particular pairing method.
What does learner catch-up measure beyond receiving the object-storage snapshot?

It asks whether the learners advance from the snapshot’s view to the required history boundary for migration. Completing an object download does not show they have accounted for writes that arrived afterward. The plan does not specify a measured catch-up time or a test outcome for either snapshot source.
Does the plan itself promise catch-up within 60 minutes?

No. It calls for comparing catch-up with direct streaming but gives no duration or result. A time bound would have to be measured or explicitly set as a condition; uploading a versioned, checksummed snapshot does not establish one by itself.
Would lower source egress be enough to prefer the object-storage approach?

The plan deliberately measures catch-up as well as egress. A reduction in source traffic would not, on its own, show that learners make the necessary progress. It also calls for fault injection at barrier promotion, so the transfer comparison is not meant to replace the ownership-boundary check. No overall choice is made here.
Why fault-inject barrier promotion after the egress and catch-up comparison?

The measurements examine the preparation path, while fault injection examines the safety-critical transition to destination authority. A learner could receive a valid snapshot and catch up yet still be unready for promotion if the required key-and-dedup barrier has not been durably installed. The plan sequences these evaluations, but does not report that either evaluation has already succeeded.
Which barrier condition must remain visible during promotion?

For the proposed ownership transfer, joint reconfiguration must wait for matching key-and-dedup barriers fsynced by a destination quorum. Fault-injecting barrier promotion should examine that boundary rather than treat a successful snapshot upload, checksum check, or learner download as a substitute for destination-quorum durability. The plan does not specify the fault schedules or report their outcomes.
Does the uploaded snapshot count as a destination-quorum-fsynced barrier?

No. Uploading a snapshot to object storage and fsyncing a matching key-and-dedup barrier at a destination quorum are different events with different purposes. The snapshot supplies a starting view for the learners; the quorum-fsynced barrier is a prerequisite for the ownership change. The plan does not equate them.
Could a correct checksum prove that deduplication state is ready for retries?

Only if an additional protocol rule established that the checked artifact contains and durably installs the relevant deduplication state, and no such rule is stated here. What kind of failure is barrier-promotion injection meant to make observable?

It should challenge whether promotion can occur when the required barrier state is incomplete or unavailable under injected faults. The pertinent safety concern is granting serving authority with key history but without matching, durable deduplication information, or otherwise failing to preserve acknowledged history. That describes what to check, not a finding that the proposed offload causes such a failure.
Can I say from this plan which replica will crash or which links will be partitioned?

No. The plan says to fault-inject barrier promotion but does not name the particular faults, their placement, or their timing. We should not supply a crash count or partition pattern as though it were specified for this activity.
What if object-storage snapshot preparation is interrupted before upload completes?

That would require the procedure to distinguish an incomplete upload from a usable versioned, checksummed snapshot. The plan does not say whether such an interruption is among the injected faults or prescribe recovery behavior. In particular, an incomplete artifact must not be assumed valid just because an upload was planned.
Does this plan already tell us whether operation throughput stays at least 80% of the migration-free baseline?

No. It calls for a source-egress and catch-up comparison, followed by barrier-promotion fault injection. Source egress is not the same quantity as operation throughput. The at-least-80% target under continuous writes without failures remains a separate performance question unless throughput is also measured and reported.
Is a faster catch-up time proof that source-quorum acknowledgments remain linearizable?

No. Catch-up time describes destination progress, not the ordering or authority of acknowledged operations. Fault-injecting the promotion boundary is relevant to safety, but even that activity is not a result until outcomes are reported. Neither a catch-up comparison nor an egress reduction alone proves linearizability.
Could the snapshot version itself decide when to jointly reconfigure?

The version identifies the snapshot artifact; it is not the stated ownership-transfer gate. Joint reconfiguration remains contingent on the destination-quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barriers. How a snapshot version relates to the barrier would need a precise rule, which this plan does not provide.

You plan to upload a versioned, checksummed copy-on-write snapshot for Raft learners, compare source egress and learner catch-up with direct streaming, and then fault-inject barrier promotion.
